weeks.title: OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs in Depth, The Two APIs That Run AI
weeks.context:
You have been using the OpenAI SDK since week 1. This week you go two layers deeper: understanding exactly how the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs differ, where they overlap, and how to write code that handles both. The project is a side-by-side chat console, type one message, get responses from both providers simultaneously, with cost and latency displayed below each.

The two APIs are not identical. OpenAI's chat completions take a messages array where the system prompt is just another message with role "system". Anthropic's Messages API takes system as a separate top-level parameter. This distinction propagates through your conversation history management, retry logic, and any abstraction layer you build. Knowing both formats also means you can convert between them, which you will need to do when the cheapest or best model for a task changes providers.

Streaming is where the experience difference becomes visceral. Both providers stream tokens, but the event formats differ slightly. OpenAI sends `data: {"choices": [{"delta": {"content": "..."}}]}`. Anthropic sends `data: {"type": "content_block_delta", "delta": {"text": "..."}}`. If you build a unified streaming handler, you need to handle both event shapes.

OpenRouter is a third option worth understanding. It proxies multiple providers through a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The tradeoff: simplified integration, single billing, but slightly higher latency, a layer of indirection in your debugging, and the risk that provider-specific features (like Anthropic's prompt caching) are unavailable or behave differently through the proxy.

The console you build this week is a tool you will genuinely use. When you hit a task later in the roadmap and are not sure whether GPT-4o or Claude will do it better, you will open this console, type the prompt, and see both responses side by side. Build it well.

concept_check.q: How does the system prompt position differ between OpenAI and Anthropic?
choices: OpenAI puts system as a message in the messages array (role='system'). Anthropic takes system as a separate top-level parameter outside the messages array
concept_check.explain: OpenAI: `messages=[{'role': 'system', 'content': '...'}, {'role': 'user', 'content': '...'}]`. Anthropic: `client.messages.create(system='...', messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': '...'}])`. Same concept; different shape. Knowing both is what lets you write code that handles both providers.

concept_check.q: Why does streaming UX feel dramatically faster even though total time-to-completion is the same?
choices: First-token latency is much shorter than total-time. Users start reading the moment the first word arrives; their perception of speed tracks first-token, not total. Streaming hides the total-time cost behind a steady scroll
concept_check.explain: Non-streaming: blank screen for 4 seconds, then everything at once. Streaming: first token at 200ms, output appearing word-by-word over 4 seconds. Same total. But the user starts READING at 200ms, their experience of latency tracks first-token, not last-token.

concept_check.q: Why use OpenRouter (or a similar proxy) instead of calling OpenAI / Anthropic directly?
choices: One OpenAI-compatible endpoint, one API key, simplified billing, and switch between 100+ models including OpenAI and Anthropic. Trade-off: extra latency hop + some provider-specific features hidden
concept_check.explain: OpenRouter proxies many providers through a single OpenAI-compatible interface. You write OpenAI-style code and can route to GPT-4o, Claude, Llama, Mistral, etc. by changing the model name. Benefits: single integration, single bill, easy A/B.

days.title: The two APIs side by side
days.summary: Same request, same output, different shapes.

items.title: Reading both API docs
items.body:
## What this week builds
A side-by-side console: type one message, see GPT-4o-mini's response on the left and Claude Haiku's response on the right, with cost + latency for each. By Sunday it deploys.

## The minimal call, OpenAI
```python
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
 model='gpt-4o-mini',
 messages=[
 {'role': 'system', 'content': 'You are a translator.'},
 {'role': 'user', 'content': 'Hello, world.'},
 ],
 temperature=0.2,
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)
print(resp.usage)
```

## The minimal call, Anthropic
```python
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()

resp = client.messages.create(
 model='claude-haiku-4-5',
 system='You are a translator.', # <-- top-level, NOT in messages
 messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': 'Hello, world.'}],
 max_tokens=200, # <-- REQUIRED for Anthropic
 temperature=0.2,
)
print(resp.content[0].text)
print(resp.usage)
```

## The four differences worth memorising
```text
1. SYSTEM PROMPT
 OpenAI: inside messages, role='system'
 Anthropic: top-level `system=` parameter

2. MAX TOKENS
 OpenAI: optional (defaults to model max)
 Anthropic: REQUIRED on every call

3. RESPONSE SHAPE
 OpenAI: resp.choices[0].message.content
 Anthropic: resp.content[0].text

4. USAGE FIELDS
 OpenAI: prompt_tokens / completion_tokens / total_tokens
 Anthropic: input_tokens / output_tokens (no 'total')
```

That's it. Anything beyond these four differences is provider-specific tuning. Knowing both shapes, and being able to convert between them, is what 'two SDKs' actually means in practice.

items.title: dual_chat.py
items.body:
## What we want
```python
# unified call signature
result = dual_chat(
 prompt='Translate to French: hello',
 system='You are a translator.',
 providers=['openai', 'anthropic'],
)
# returns [{'provider': 'openai', 'text': 'Bonjour', 'usage': {...}, 'cost': 0.000003, 'latency_ms': 412},
# {'provider': 'anthropic', 'text': 'Bonjour', 'usage': {...}, 'cost': 0.000002, 'latency_ms': 350}]
```

## Implementation
```python
# console/dual_chat.py
import os, time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from openai import OpenAI
from anthropic import Anthropic

_oai = OpenAI()
_anth = Anthropic()

# per-million-token rates. Update if pricing changes.
OPENAI_MODEL = 'gpt-4o-mini'
OPENAI_IN_RATE = 0.15 / 1_000_000
OPENAI_OUT_RATE = 0.60 / 1_000_000

ANTH_MODEL = 'claude-haiku-4-5'
ANTH_IN_RATE = 0.25 / 1_000_000 # update from anthropic.com/pricing
ANTH_OUT_RATE = 1.25 / 1_000_000

def _call_openai(prompt: str, system: str):
 t0 = time.time()
 resp = _oai.chat.completions.create(
 model=OPENAI_MODEL,
 messages=[
 {'role': 'system', 'content': system},
 {'role': 'user', 'content': prompt},
 ],
 temperature=0.2,
 )
 dt = int((time.time() - t0) * 1000)
 cost = resp.usage.prompt_tokens * OPENAI_IN_RATE + resp.usage.completion_tokens * OPENAI_OUT_RATE
 return {
 'provider': 'openai',
 'model': OPENAI_MODEL,
 'text': resp.choices[0].message.content.strip(),
 'usage': {'input': resp.usage.prompt_tokens, 'output': resp.usage.completion_tokens},
 'cost': cost,
 'latency_ms': dt,
 }

def _call_anthropic(prompt: str, system: str):
 t0 = time.time()
 resp = _anth.messages.create(
 model=ANTH_MODEL,
 system=system,
 messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': prompt}],
 max_tokens=1024,
 temperature=0.2,
 )
 dt = int((time.time() - t0) * 1000)
 cost = resp.usage.input_tokens * ANTH_IN_RATE + resp.usage.output_tokens * ANTH_OUT_RATE
 return {
 'provider': 'anthropic',
 'model': ANTH_MODEL,
 'text': resp.content[0].text.strip(),
 'usage': {'input': resp.usage.input_tokens, 'output': resp.usage.output_tokens},
 'cost': cost,
 'latency_ms': dt,
 }

def dual_chat(prompt: str, system: str, providers=('openai', 'anthropic')):
 fns = {'openai': _call_openai, 'anthropic': _call_anthropic}
 with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=len(providers)) as ex:
 futures = {p: ex.submit(fns[p], prompt, system) for p in providers}
 return [futures[p].result() for p in providers]
```

## Why ThreadPoolExecutor
Calling them sequentially: 1.5s + 1.5s = 3s wall time. In parallel: max(1.5, 1.5) ≈ 1.5s. The two API calls are independent; running them in parallel halves the user-visible latency. `ThreadPoolExecutor` is the simplest possible parallelism, no asyncio, no callbacks.

## Test it
```bash
python -c "from dual_chat import dual_chat; import json; print(json.dumps(dual_chat('What is 2+2?', 'You are concise.'), indent=2))"
```

cards.prompt: Running both API calls in parallel halves the wall-clock latency the user sees.
cards.whenRight: Right, max(a, b) instead of a+b. Independent calls = parallel.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, parallel halves visible latency. ThreadPoolExecutor is sufficient; no asyncio needed.

cards.prompt: Returning a unified shape (provider, text, usage, cost, latency_ms) hides the SDK differences from any caller.
cards.whenRight: Right, adapter pattern. Caller doesn't care which SDK ran underneath.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, unified shape = abstraction. The console UI just renders the shape; the SDK quirks live in dual_chat.

cards.prompt: Anthropic pricing rates are the same as OpenAI's, so you can use one rate for both.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Each provider/model has its own per-million-token rate. Pull from the pricing page; update when rates change.
cards.whenWrong: Different per-token. Maintain rates per (provider, model). Cost truth requires per-model rate constants.

items.title: Streaming side by side
items.body:
## OpenAI streaming
```python
stream = _oai.chat.completions.create(
 model=OPENAI_MODEL,
 messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': prompt}],
 stream=True,
)
for chunk in stream:
 delta = chunk.choices[0].delta.content
 if delta:
 print(delta, end='', flush=True)
```

## Anthropic streaming
```python
with _anth.messages.stream(
 model=ANTH_MODEL,
 system=system,
 messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': prompt}],
 max_tokens=1024,
) as stream:
 for text in stream.text_stream:
 print(text, end='', flush=True)
```

Anthropic's SDK gives you a clean `text_stream` iterator that yields plain strings. OpenAI's gives you chunks with delta objects you have to unwrap. Different ergonomics for the same idea.

## Why streaming matters perceptually
Non-streaming UX: user clicks Send, screen blank for 3-5 seconds, full answer appears. Feels slow.

Streaming UX: user clicks Send, first words appear in 200-400ms, more text scrolls in over 3-5 seconds. Same total time, but the user starts READING immediately. Perceived latency tracks first-token, not last-token.

Every consumer LLM product streams. ChatGPT streams. Claude streams. Cursor streams. If you're building anything user-facing, streaming is non-negotiable.

## What you measure
```text
- TTFT (Time To First Token), the perceived-speed number
- TPS (Tokens Per Second), sustained generation speed
- Total time, the bill
```

Print all three when you run streaming calls. The numbers tell you which provider feels fast and which is fast.

cards.prompt: Streaming reduces total response time.
cards.whenRight: Right, no. Same total. Streaming reduces PERCEIVED time because the user starts reading at first-token.
cards.whenWrong: Total is the same; perception isn't. Streaming reshapes the user's experience of latency.

cards.prompt: Anthropic's `messages.stream()` exposes `text_stream`, a clean iterator of plain strings.
cards.whenRight: Right, ergonomic. OpenAI's chunks-with-deltas needs more unwrapping.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, text_stream is the clean handle. Anthropic's streaming ergonomics are slightly more pleasant for plain text.

cards.prompt: Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) is the metric that tracks perceived speed.
cards.whenRight: Right, TTFT = the headline number for UX feel. Sub-second is the goal for chat-style UIs.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, TTFT is what the user feels. Total time is what the bill measures.

items.title: console_app.py
items.body:
## What it does
Single text area at the top. 'Send' button. Two columns: left for OpenAI, right for Anthropic. Each column shows the response, cost, latency. Sidebar shows session totals + lets you switch which model each side uses.

## Minimal version
```python
# console/app.py
import streamlit as st
from dual_chat import dual_chat

st.set_page_config(page_title='Dual console', layout='wide')
st.title('OpenAI vs Anthropic, side-by-side console')

system = st.sidebar.text_area('System prompt', value='You are concise.', height=120)

prompt = st.text_area('Your message', height=140)
send = st.button('Send', type='primary', disabled=not prompt.strip())

if 'history' not in st.session_state:
 st.session_state.history = []

if send:
 with st.spinner('Calling both providers in parallel…'):
 results = dual_chat(prompt, system)
 st.session_state.history.insert(0, {'prompt': prompt, 'results': results})

for turn in st.session_state.history[:5]:
 st.markdown(f'**You:** {turn["prompt"]}')
 cols = st.columns(2)
 for col, r in zip(cols, turn['results']):
 with col:
 st.markdown(f'### {r["provider"]} · `{r["model"]}`')
 st.write(r['text'])
 st.caption(
 f'{r["usage"]["input"]} → {r["usage"]["output"]} tok · '
 f'${r["cost"]:.6f} · {r["latency_ms"]}ms'
 )
 st.divider()

# session totals
flat = [r for turn in st.session_state.history for r in turn['results']]
by_provider = {}
for r in flat:
 bp = by_provider.setdefault(r['provider'], {'cost': 0, 'calls': 0, 'tokens': 0})
 bp['cost'] += r['cost']
 bp['calls'] += 1
 bp['tokens'] += r['usage']['input'] + r['usage']['output']

with st.sidebar:
 st.markdown('---')
 st.markdown('### Session totals')
 for p, t in by_provider.items():
 st.metric(f'{p} cost', f'${t["cost"]:.6f}')
 st.caption(f'{t["calls"]} calls · {t["tokens"]:,} tokens')
```

## Run it
```bash
streamlit run console/app.py
```

## What this becomes
A tool you ACTUALLY USE later in the roadmap. Whenever you're picking between models for a task, open the console, type the prompt, see both side by side. Live tool > theoretical comparison.

cards.prompt: Side-by-side layouts use `st.columns(2)` to split the width 50/50.
cards.whenRight: Right, st.columns(N) gives N equal columns. Two of them for left/right comparison.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, st.columns(2) is the call. Easy 50/50 split for comparison UIs.

cards.prompt: Tracking per-provider session totals lets you see which one is cheaper for your actual workload.
cards.whenRight: Right, real numbers > pricing-page estimates. Your workload IS the test.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, real-usage totals. Pricing pages give per-token; your console gives per-session.

cards.prompt: Storing the full history in `st.session_state` is enough, no DB needed for a personal console.
cards.whenRight: Right, session_state is enough for a personal dev tool. DB would be over-engineering.
cards.whenWrong: Yes, session_state for personal scope. DB matters only when state persists across sessions.

items.title: Function calling, what it is
items.body:
## The idea
You define a function ('get_weather(city)'). You tell the model it exists. When the user asks 'What's the weather in Banjul?', the model decides 'I should call get_weather with city=Banjul' and returns a structured request, not free text. Your code calls the actual function, gets the result, hands it back to the model, which then writes a natural-language reply.

This is the foundation of every agent / RAG / structured-tool LLM you'll touch later.

## OpenAI shape
```python
tools = [{
 'type': 'function',
 'function': {
 'name': 'get_weather',
 'description': 'Get current weather for a city',
 'parameters': {
 'type': 'object',
 'properties': {'city': {'type': 'string'}},
 'required': ['city'],
 },
 },
}]

resp = _oai.chat.completions.create(
 model='gpt-4o-mini',
 messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': 'What\'s the weather in Banjul?'}],
 tools=tools,
)
tool_calls = resp.choices[0].message.tool_calls
# tool_calls[0].function.name == 'get_weather'
# tool_calls[0].function.arguments == '{"city": "Banjul"}'
```

## Anthropic shape
```python
tools = [{
 'name': 'get_weather',
 'description': 'Get current weather for a city',
 'input_schema': {
 'type': 'object',
 'properties': {'city': {'type': 'string'}},
 'required': ['city'],
 },
}]

resp = _anth.messages.create(
 model='claude-haiku-4-5',
 max_tokens=1024,
 tools=tools,
 messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': 'What\'s the weather in Banjul?'}],
)
for block in resp.content:
 if block.type == 'tool_use':
 # block.name == 'get_weather'
 # block.input == {'city': 'Banjul'}
 pass
```

## The differences worth memorising
```text
OpenAI: tools is a list of {type:'function', function:{name, description, parameters: <jsonschema>}}
 call appears at resp.choices[0].message.tool_calls
 args is a JSON STRING (you json.loads it)

Anthropic: tools is a list of {name, description, input_schema: <jsonschema>}
 call appears as a 'tool_use' block in resp.content
 args is already a Python dict
```

Same JSON Schema for parameters; everything else differs.

## The agent loop
```text
1. Call model with tools + user message.
2. Model says: 'I want to call get_weather(city="Banjul")'.
3. Your code runs get_weather('Banjul') → '32°C, sunny'.
4. Call the model AGAIN with the original messages + the tool result.
5. Model writes the natural reply: 'It's 32°C and sunny in Banjul today.'
```

That loop is the foundation of every LLM agent. Master it on a toy `get_weather` today; the next 20 weeks of the roadmap build on it.

days.title: OpenRouter, the proxy option
days.summary: When to use a unified gateway instead of native SDKs.

items.title: What OpenRouter is
items.body:
## In one line
OpenRouter is an OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint that proxies to 100+ models from many providers. You write OpenAI-shape code; you route by changing the `model=` string.

## Using it
```python
from openai import OpenAI

router = OpenAI(
 base_url='https://openrouter.ai/api/v1',
 api_key=os.environ['OPENROUTER_API_KEY'],
)

# Now switch providers just by changing the model name:
r1 = router.chat.completions.create(model='openai/gpt-4o-mini', messages=[...])
r2 = router.chat.completions.create(model='anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5', messages=[...])
r3 = router.chat.completions.create(model='meta-llama/llama-3.1-70b', messages=[...])
```

Same code shape, anywhere you wrote OpenAI calls, you can swap models. One API key, one billing dashboard, immediate access to providers that don't normally let you sign up directly.

## The trade-offs
```text
Pros:
- One integration, many models.
- Single key + single bill, useful for solo builders.
- Easy A/B between models, even cross-provider.
- Access to community fine-tunes you'd struggle to host yourself.

Cons:
- Extra hop: typically 50-200ms more latency than native.
- Provider-specific features may not pass through (Anthropic prompt caching,
 Anthropic 'pdf' content blocks, OpenAI Responses API features).
- Pricing usually adds a small markup over native.
- Outages at OpenRouter affect ALL your providers at once (single point of failure).
```

## When to use which
```text
Use the native SDKs (OpenAI / Anthropic directly):
- Production with strict latency budgets.
- Need provider-specific features (prompt caching, structured outputs).
- You already maintain accounts at the providers.

Use OpenRouter:
- Prototyping / experimentation across many models.
- One-person projects where dual-billing is painful.
- Polyglot-style A/B comparisons across providers.
```

## Practical try
Add a third column to your console, same prompt, routed via OpenRouter to a model you couldn't easily call natively (e.g. `meta-llama/llama-3.1-70b-instruct`). Now you have 3-way comparison.

weeks.title: Structured Outputs, Making LLMs Return JSON You Can Actually Trust
weeks.context:
Language models are text generators. When you need structured data, a JSON object, a list of extracted entities, a form with typed fields, you cannot rely on asking nicely and hoping the model formats it correctly. JSON mode helps. Schema-enforced function calling helps more. The instructor library makes the whole thing reliable. This week you build an invoice parser that turns images of real invoices into structured Pydantic objects with a measurable success rate.

The fundamental insight is that Pydantic models serve two purposes simultaneously: they validate the output you receive, and they define the schema that tells the model what to produce. When you pass a Pydantic model to instructor, it extracts the JSON schema from the model definition, constructs the appropriate tool-use call or response format parameter, and automatically retries if the response fails validation. You write the model once and get both validation and structured prompting from it.

Failure modes in structured output are important to understand because they occur in production even with the best models. The model invents a field that does not exist in your schema. It puts a string where you expected a number. It drops a required field when the source document is ambiguous. It returns a list when you expected a single object. Each of these requires a different mitigation strategy.

The invoice parser is a strong portfolio project because it solves a real business problem. Every company processes invoices. The ability to extract structured data from unstructured documents, receipts, contracts, medical records, shipping manifests, is high-value and broadly applicable. Build it well, measure it honestly, and you have something worth showing.

concept_check.q: You define an Invoice Pydantic model with a `line_items: list[LineItem]` field. The invoice image has three items but the model returns only two. Is this a structured output failure or a vision failur?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

concept_check.q: instructor's auto-retry fires when validation fails. What does it send to the model on the retry? It sends the original prompt plus the validation error message as additional context. For example: "Va?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

concept_check.q: Your invoice parser succeeds on 4 out of 5 invoices. The 5th invoice has a handwritten amount and an unusual format. What do you report? Report all of this in your accuracy measurement: 4/5 structured?

items.title: Set up your tooling
items.body:

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
Language models generate text, and text is exactly the wrong thing to hand to the rest of your program. When the next step is "save this to a database" or "call an API with these fields," you need a typed object, not a paragraph that probably contains the data. This week you build an invoice parser: feed it a real invoice, get back a validated `Invoice` object (vendor, date, line items, total) with a success rate you can measure. By Sunday you understand the whole reliability ladder, from "ask nicely for JSON" to schema-enforced outputs, and you can make a model return structured data you actually trust.

## Why "just ask for JSON" is not enough
The naive approach is to put "respond in JSON" in the prompt and parse the result. It works until it doesn't: the model wraps the JSON in fences, adds a "Here is the data:" preamble, omits a field, invents a field, or returns `"N/A"` where you expected a number. Every one of those is a crash or a silent bug downstream. The whole week is about climbing from that fragile baseline to outputs that are structurally guaranteed, because a parser that works 95% of the time is a parser that fails on one invoice in twenty, which at any real volume means it fails constantly.

## The central idea: one schema, two jobs
The thing that makes this click is a Pydantic model doing double duty. When you write `class Invoice(BaseModel)`, that single definition (a) describes the schema you send to the model so it knows exactly what fields and types to produce, and (b) validates the response when it comes back, coercing types and rejecting anything malformed. Your data shape is defined once, in Python, and it both instructs the model and guards your program. Hold that idea, the model IS the schema, and every tool this week (JSON mode, function calling, the `instructor` library) is just a different way of wiring it up.

## Where this fits
You build the invoice parser this week and measure how often it produces a valid, correct `Invoice`. Structured output is the foundation everything later depends on: an agent's tool calls (W13) are structured outputs, RAG's metadata filters are structured outputs, and a production AI feature that cannot reliably hand typed data to the next system is not shippable. This is the week the model stops returning prose and starts returning data.

items.title: JSON mode
items.body:
## The first rung: guarantee valid JSON
The lowest reliable rung above "ask nicely" is JSON mode, a flag that guarantees the model returns syntactically valid, parseable JSON, no fences, no preamble, no trailing prose. In the OpenAI SDK it is one parameter:
```python
from openai import OpenAI
import json
client = OpenAI()

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},   # guarantees valid JSON
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "Extract invoice fields. Reply with JSON."},
        {"role": "user", "content": invoice_text},
    ],
)
data = json.loads(resp.choices[0].message.content)   # safe: the string parses
```
The `json.loads` is now safe: JSON mode guarantees the string parses. That removes an entire class of failure, the malformed-string crash.

## What JSON mode does NOT give you
JSON mode is necessary and not sufficient, and understanding the gap is the point. It guarantees the output is valid JSON; it does NOT guarantee the output matches your schema. The model can still return `{"vendor": "Acme"}` when you needed five fields, or `{"total": "forty dollars"}` when you needed a number, or invent a `{"notes": "..."}` field you never asked for. JSON mode fixes the syntax problem and leaves the shape problem completely open. So it is a real improvement (your parser stops crashing on fenced output) and only the first rung: you still have to validate that the valid JSON is the JSON you wanted.

## You must still describe the shape in the prompt
There is a sharp gotcha with JSON mode: most implementations require the word "JSON" to appear in your prompt, and none of them infer your fields, so you still have to tell the model what JSON you want in words. With bare JSON mode, your field list lives in the prompt as prose ("return vendor, invoice_date, total as a number, and a list of line_items"), which is brittle, the prompt and your actual data shape drift apart, and nothing enforces the match. That brittleness is exactly the problem the next lesson solves by moving the shape out of the prompt and into a Pydantic model that is the single source of truth.

## Where this fits
Use JSON mode to get your invoice parser returning parseable JSON, then deliberately feed it a messy invoice and watch it return valid JSON that is missing a field or has the total as a string. Seeing valid-but-wrong output is the motivation for the rest of the week: syntax is solved, but trusting the shape needs the schema enforcement you build next.

items.title: Pydantic v2 models as the source of truth for both validation and prompt schema
items.body:
## Define the data once, in Python
This is the conceptual heart of the week. Instead of describing your invoice shape in prose inside the prompt, you define it once as a Pydantic model, and that model becomes the single source of truth for both the request and the response:
```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from datetime import date

class LineItem(BaseModel):
    description: str
    quantity: int
    unit_price: float

class Invoice(BaseModel):
    vendor: str = Field(description="The company that issued the invoice")
    invoice_date: date
    line_items: list[LineItem]
    total: float = Field(description="The grand total in the invoice's currency")
```
Two things this buys you at once. Pydantic emits this as a JSON Schema (`Invoice.model_json_schema()`) to send to the model, so the model sees exactly the fields and types you expect. And Pydantic validates any dict against it (`Invoice.model_validate(data)`), coercing `"3"` to `3`, parsing the date string, and raising a clear error if `total` is missing. One definition, both jobs.

## Why the field descriptions matter
The `Field(description=...)` annotations are not documentation for you, they are instructions to the model. When Pydantic generates the schema, those descriptions travel with each field, so "The grand total in the invoice's currency" tells the model which number to pick when an invoice has a subtotal, a tax line, and a total. Writing good field descriptions is the new prompt engineering for structured output: vague field names produce vague extraction, and a one-line description on the ambiguous fields (which date, which total, what format) is usually the difference between a parser that gets it right and one that guesses.

## Validation is where reliability actually lives
The payoff of the model-as-schema is that validation catches the model's mistakes before they reach your program. Feed the LLM's JSON through `Invoice.model_validate(data)` and one of two things happens: it returns a typed `Invoice` you can trust (`invoice.total` is genuinely a float, `invoice.invoice_date` is a real `date`), or it raises a `ValidationError` that tells you exactly which field was wrong. That error is not a failure, it is a signal, the hook the next lesson uses to automatically ask the model to fix its own output. Without validation you discover the bad `total` three systems downstream; with it, you catch it at the boundary.

## Where this fits
Define your `Invoice` and `LineItem` models with real field descriptions, generate the JSON Schema from them, and validate a model response through them. You now have your data shape defined once, instructing the model and guarding your code, which is the structure the `instructor` library automates into a single clean call.

items.title: Anthropic's tool use for structured outputs
items.body:
## The same goal, the schema-enforced way
JSON mode guarantees valid JSON; schema-enforced structured output guarantees the JSON matches your model. Both major providers offer it, and Anthropic's path runs through tool use, which is worth understanding because it is the same mechanism agents use later (W13). The trick: you define a "tool" whose input schema IS your Pydantic schema, and force the model to "call" it, so the model's only valid move is to emit arguments matching your schema exactly.
```python
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-haiku-4-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=[{
        "name": "record_invoice",
        "description": "Record the structured fields of an invoice",
        "input_schema": Invoice.model_json_schema(),
    }],
    tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "record_invoice"},   # force the schema
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": invoice_text}],
)
data = resp.content[0].input               # the schema-matching dict
invoice = Invoice.model_validate(data)     # validate to be safe
```
By forcing `tool_choice` to your tool, you have removed the model's freedom to reply with prose or the wrong shape; its only option is to fill in your schema.

## The two-provider reality
Notice what changed and what didn't between this and yesterday's OpenAI code. The API surface differs: Anthropic puts the schema in a `tools` array and forces it with `tool_choice`, where OpenAI has a dedicated structured-outputs `response_format`; Anthropic also takes the system prompt as a top-level parameter, not a message. But the Pydantic model is identical, `Invoice.model_json_schema()` feeds both. This is the W5 lesson paying off: the providers differ at the wiring, and your data definition is portable across them. Real AI products often call both providers, and the thing that stays constant is your schema.

## Newer first-class structured outputs
Tool use is the durable, widely-supported way to get schema-enforced output from Claude, and the API also offers structured outputs more directly: you pass an `output_config` with your JSON Schema format and let the SDK validate the response against it (the SDK's `messages.parse()` helper does this and hands you a parsed object). It is cleaner when available, and the tool-use pattern remains the one to understand deeply, because it is identical to how you give a model actions in the agents phase. Either way the principle is the same as the rest of the week: the schema constrains the output, and you validate on the way in.

## Where this fits
Wire your invoice parser to Claude via forced tool use with your `Invoice` schema, and confirm the same Pydantic model that drove the OpenAI call drives this one. You have now seen schema-enforced output on both providers and learned the tool-use mechanism you will reuse for agents, with your data definition portable across both.

items.title: Schema design
items.body:
## The schema is a contract you have to design
By now the mechanism is solved; the skill that separates a reliable parser from a flaky one is designing the schema well. A schema is a contract between you and the model, and small choices change the success rate a lot. The biggest lever is making the schema express what is actually true about your data, including the messy parts:
- **Optional fields for things that may be absent.** Not every invoice has a PO number. `po_number: str | None = None` lets the model say "not present" honestly instead of inventing one.
- **Enums for fixed sets.** `currency: Literal["USD", "EUR", "GBP"]` constrains the model to valid values and rejects a hallucinated `"dollars"`.
- **Nested models for repeated structure.** `line_items: list[LineItem]` is far more reliable than asking for a free-form string and parsing it yourself.

## Model the ambiguity, don't paper over it
The mistake that tanks extraction accuracy is forcing a clean schema onto dirty reality. If a field is sometimes missing and you mark it required, the model is forced to fabricate a value to satisfy the schema, you have designed the hallucination in. The fix is to let the schema admit uncertainty: optional fields for maybe-absent data, a `confidence` field where you want the model to flag a shaky read, a `notes` field for context that doesn't fit elsewhere. A schema that can represent "I'm not sure" or "this isn't here" gets you honest output; a rigid schema with no way to say those things gets you confident-sounding garbage.

## Descriptions and constraints do real work
Two more design tools earn their place. Descriptions disambiguate (which "date", which "total"), and matter more as fields get more alike. Constraints catch errors structurally: `quantity: int = Field(ge=1)` rejects a zero-quantity line item, `total: float = Field(gt=0)` rejects a negative grand total, and Pydantic enforces these on validation so a violating extraction surfaces as a clear error rather than bad data. The discipline is to encode what you know about valid invoices into the schema, so the schema itself rejects impossible outputs instead of you writing checks after the fact.

## Where this fits
Redesign your `Invoice` schema to match real invoices: optional fields for what's sometimes missing, an enum for currency, constraints on quantities and totals, and sharp descriptions on the ambiguous fields. Then run it against a handful of genuinely messy invoices and watch the success rate move. Schema design is the highest-leverage skill in structured output, and it is mostly about honestly modelling how messy the real data is.

items.title: Streaming structured outputs
items.body:
## Why stream something structured at all
Structured output and streaming feel opposed, you cannot validate half an object, but there is a real reason to combine them: perceived latency. Extracting a big invoice with twenty line items can take several seconds, and a user staring at a spinner feels every one. Streaming lets you show the object filling in as the model produces it, vendor appears, then the date, then line items one by one, so the interface feels alive even though the total time is the same. For a structured-output product with a UI, streaming is the difference between "frozen" and "working."

## Partial validation: the model fills in as it goes
The mechanism is partial validation: as tokens arrive, you repeatedly attempt to parse the incomplete JSON into a partial version of your model, and render whatever fields are populated so far. You do not hand-roll this, the `instructor` library (tomorrow's tool, previewed here) supports it directly by yielding a stream of progressively-more-complete model instances:
```python
stream = client.chat.completions.create_partial(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    response_model=Invoice,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": invoice_text}],
)
for partial in stream:           # each is an Invoice with more fields filled in
    render(partial)              # vendor first, then date, then line_items...
```
Each `partial` is a valid-so-far `Invoice`; your UI re-renders as it grows. The final one is the complete, fully-validated object.

## When streaming structured output is worth it, and when it isn't
Be deliberate, because streaming adds complexity. It earns its keep when a human is watching the result form in a UI, a chat assistant extracting data live, a tool showing a document being parsed, because the responsiveness is real and felt. It is pointless when the consumer is another program: a backend job parsing 10,000 invoices does not care about partial objects, it wants the final validated result, and streaming just complicates the code. The rule mirrors the engineering-judgement theme of the track: add streaming where a person experiences the latency, skip it where a machine consumes the output.

## Where this fits
Add streaming to your invoice parser's UI so the `Invoice` visibly fills in as it is extracted, using partial validation. You have now handled structured output end to end, valid JSON, schema enforcement, good schema design, and a responsive UI, which is the full toolkit for making a model return data you can trust and a product that feels fast while it does.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
Your invoice parser turns real invoices into validated `Invoice` objects, with a number attached. By tonight:
- a Pydantic `Invoice` schema is the single source of truth, instructing the model and validating its output.
- the parser uses schema-enforced output (forced tool use on Claude, or structured outputs / `instructor`), not bare "please return JSON."
- the schema honestly models messy invoices, optional fields, enums, constraints, so the model is not forced to fabricate.
- you have a measured success rate on a set of test invoices, not a vibe.

## The test that proves it: measure it
The deliverable that makes this real is the number. Collect ten to twenty real invoices (with the correct fields written down by hand), run them through your parser, and compute how often it produces a valid `Invoice` whose fields match the truth. "My parser is 90% accurate on 20 invoices, and the failures are all on handwritten totals" is the exact sentence structured-output work is supposed to produce, it tells you the parser works AND where it breaks. A parser you have measured is a tool; a parser you assume works is a liability. That habit, building a small labelled set and scoring against it, is the seed of the evals discipline you build properly in W12 and W17.

## Ship the artifact
Commit the parser with its Pydantic schema, a few example invoices, and a short README stating the measured success rate and the known failure modes. The schema and the score are the portfolio piece: they show you can make an LLM produce typed, validated data reliably, which is the single most common real-world AI-engineering task, every "extract X from documents" feature is this. Anyone can get JSON out of a model once; demonstrating a measured, schema-enforced parser shows you can do it in production.

## Where this fits in the track

weeks.title: Streaming and Cost, Two Levers That Make or Break a Product
weeks.context:
Two things determine whether an AI feature feels good to users: how fast it responds and how much it costs to operate. Streaming addresses the first, a response that appears word by word feels faster than a response that appears all at once after a 4-second wait, even if the total time is identical. Cost decomposition addresses the second, you cannot optimise what you do not measure.

This week you build a cost dashboard that reads from a SQLite database and visualises per-day cost, per-model cost, per-feature cost, and the top 10 most expensive individual requests. More importantly, you instrument one of your existing projects so that every API call writes a record to this database. By the end of the week, you have a live view of exactly what your AI usage costs.

Streaming is technically simple, the SDK provides an iterator that yields chunks, but the implementation details matter. Markdown rendering requires buffering: you cannot render a heading until you have seen the closing newline. Code blocks require detecting the opening triple-backtick before you know what language to highlight. JSON streaming requires handling partial JSON that may not be valid until the stream completes. Each of these is a real problem you will encounter in production.

The economics of AI APIs have a structure worth understanding deeply. Input tokens typically cost 3-4x less than output tokens. Prompt caching (available on both major providers) gives you a significant discount on cache-read tokens when the same prefix is reused. Model routing, using a smaller, cheaper model for simple queries, can reduce costs by 80% with minimal quality loss. These levers only work if you have instrumented your costs well enough to know where the money is going.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
Two numbers decide whether an AI feature is usable: how fast it feels, and how much it costs to run. This week you make both visible and controllable. You build a cost dashboard backed by SQLite that shows per-day, per-model, and per-feature spend plus your ten most expensive individual requests, and you instrument one of your existing projects so every API call writes a record to it. By Sunday you have a live, honest view of what your AI usage costs, and you have learned the levers, streaming for speed, caching and routing and batching for cost, that turn a working demo into something you can actually afford to ship.

## Why these two levers and not the model
Beginners obsess over which model is smartest. Products live or die on the two boring things instead. Streaming addresses perceived speed: a response that appears word by word feels fast even when the total time is unchanged, and a four-second silent wait feels broken even when the answer is good. Cost addresses whether the feature survives contact with real traffic: an AI feature that delights ten users can bankrupt you at ten thousand if nobody measured the per-request cost. Neither is about model quality, and both are squarely the AI engineer's job, the part a data scientist or a prompt tinkerer usually does not think about.

## The rule that governs the whole week: measure first
The thread tying streaming and cost together is that you cannot improve what you have not instrumented. You do not guess what your AI costs; you log the actual token usage of every call, because every response from both providers reports exactly how many input, output, and cached tokens it used. That `usage` data, written to your SQLite database per call, is the ground truth the dashboard reads. Optimisation without measurement is superstition, "I think caching helped" is worthless; "caching cut my per-request cost from $0.04 to $0.006, here's the dashboard" is engineering. Build the measurement first, then pull the levers and watch the numbers move.

## Where this fits
You instrument cost across your existing projects this week and learn to stream responses. This is the operational backbone of every AI product you build after: the agents (W13), RAG systems (W9), and production features (W17-20) all run on these same levers, and a feature you have not cost-instrumented is a feature you cannot responsibly put in front of users. Last week the model returned trustworthy data; this week it returns it fast and affordably.

items.title: Token streaming
items.body:
## The model produces tokens one at a time; show them that way
A model generates its response token by token, and by default the SDK waits for the whole thing before handing it to you. Streaming asks for those tokens as they are produced, so you can render the answer as it appears. The SDKs make the basic case trivial:
```python
# OpenAI
stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain streaming in two sentences."}],
    stream=True,
)
for chunk in stream:
    delta = chunk.choices[0].delta.content or ""
    print(delta, end="", flush=True)
```
```python
# Anthropic
with client.messages.stream(model="claude-haiku-4-5", max_tokens=512,
                            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "..."}]) as stream:
    for text in stream.text_stream:
        print(text, end="", flush=True)
    final = stream.get_final_message()   # full message + usage when done
```
The `flush=True` matters; without it your terminal buffers and the streaming effect disappears.

## Why streaming is mostly a perception win, with one real one
Be precise about what streaming buys you. It does NOT make the model faster, the total generation time is identical. What it changes is time to first token: the user sees something happening in a few hundred milliseconds instead of staring at nothing for four seconds, and a response that visibly grows reads as responsive even when it is not quicker. That perception is worth a lot in a chat UI. There is also one genuine, non-perceptual benefit: for long outputs, streaming avoids request timeouts, a two-minute generation that would time out as a single blocking call streams fine because bytes keep arriving. So you stream for felt speed in interactive products, and out of necessity for long generations.

## Get the final message and the usage, not just the deltas
A streaming mistake that bites people: they print the deltas and throw away the metadata. You still need the complete assembled text (to save it, to validate it) and the token `usage` (for this week's cost dashboard), and a streamed response delivers both at the end. The OpenAI stream's final chunk carries the finish reason and, when requested, usage; the Anthropic SDK's `get_final_message()` hands you the whole `Message` including `usage`. Always capture the final message, streaming is how you display the response, not an excuse to lose the structured result you would have gotten from a blocking call. This is exactly the seam you will use to log every call's cost.

## Where this fits
Add streaming to one of your interactive projects (the chat console from W5 is ideal), printing tokens as they arrive while still capturing the final message and its usage. You have the speed lever in hand, and the `usage` you capture at the end of each stream is the raw material for the cost instrumentation you build the rest of the week.

items.title: Buffering and flushing
items.body:
## Raw tokens are not always renderable
Printing tokens straight to a terminal works; rendering them into formatted output does not, because formats have structure that spans many tokens. You cannot render a Markdown heading until you have seen the line that closes it; you cannot syntax-highlight a code block until you have seen its opening fence and language tag; you cannot draw a table until the row is complete. Each of these is a real production problem: the model streams `## My head` then `ing`, and a naive renderer either flashes a broken heading or shows the raw hashes. The fix is buffering, you accumulate tokens until you have a renderable unit, then flush it.

## The buffer-and-flush pattern
The shape is always the same: append each token to a buffer, decide when the buffer contains something you can safely render, render it, and clear up to that point.
```python
buffer = ""
for delta in stream_text():
    buffer += delta
    while "\n" in buffer:                 # a complete line is renderable
        line, buffer = buffer.split("\n", 1)
        render_markdown_line(line)        # now safe to format headings, lists, etc.
render_markdown_line(buffer)              # flush the remainder at the end
```
The granularity is a judgement call: line-by-line is the common unit for Markdown, but a code block needs you to track that you are inside a fence and buffer the whole block until the closing fence. The skill is choosing a flush boundary that is both safe to render and small enough to still feel live.

## The tension: responsiveness vs correctness
Buffering trades the very thing streaming gave you, immediacy, against correctness, so the engineering is in balancing them. Flush too eagerly (every token) and you get broken half-rendered formatting; buffer too much (wait for the whole response) and you have thrown away streaming entirely and are back to the blocking experience. The right boundary depends on the format and the surface: a plain-text chat can flush every token, a Markdown renderer flushes per line, a code block flushes per complete block. Naming that tension, and picking the smallest safe unit for your output format, is the actual content of this lesson, and it is the kind of detail that separates a polished streaming UI from one that flickers.

## Where this fits
Take your streaming output and render it as Markdown, buffering by line and handling code blocks as whole units, so the formatted result builds smoothly instead of flashing broken syntax. You now have streaming that looks production-grade, not just a raw token dump, which is the difference between a demo and a chat interface a user would actually trust.

items.title: Input vs output token economics
items.body:
## Tokens are the unit of cost, and not all tokens cost the same
Every API call is billed in tokens, and the single most important fact about LLM cost is that output tokens cost several times more than input tokens, typically three to five times. Concretely, a model might charge $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output, so the answer the model writes is far more expensive per token than the prompt you send. This asymmetry shapes every cost decision: a long prompt is cheap, a long response is not, and "make the model more concise" is often a bigger cost win than "shorten the prompt." Knowing the ratio for the models you use is the starting point for reasoning about spend at all.

## Read the real numbers off the response
You do not estimate token usage, you read it, because every response reports it exactly. Both providers return a `usage` object with the input and output token counts (and cached counts) for that call:
```python
resp = client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4o-mini", messages=[...])
u = resp.usage
cost = (u.prompt_tokens * IN_RATE + u.completion_tokens * OUT_RATE) / 1_000_000
log_call(model="gpt-4o-mini", in_tok=u.prompt_tokens,
         out_tok=u.completion_tokens, cost=cost, feature="invoice_parser")
```
This is the ground truth your dashboard runs on: per call, log the model, the input and output tokens, the computed cost, and a feature tag. Estimation tools like `tiktoken` are fine for a rough pre-flight guess on OpenAI models, but for accounting you log the actual `usage` the API charged you for, never a guess (and `tiktoken` does not match non-OpenAI tokenizers, so the API's own count is the only number you can trust across providers).

## Where the money actually goes, and the levers
Once you are logging real usage tagged by feature, the dashboard tells you something you cannot guess: which feature, which model, which handful of requests dominate the bill. The pattern is almost always lopsided, a few expensive features, or a long-context call repeated thousands of times. That visibility is what makes the cost levers actionable: shorten verbose outputs (the expensive token), route simple requests to a cheaper model, cache repeated prompt prefixes (tomorrow), or batch non-urgent work (D6). None of these is worth applying blind; with per-feature cost in front of you, you optimise the line that actually costs money instead of the one that feels expensive.

## Where this fits
Instrument one project to log every call's real `usage` and computed cost into your SQLite database, tagged by feature, and confirm the numbers add up against your provider's billing page. You now have the measurement layer the whole week depends on, and the input/output asymmetry in mind, which together turn cost from an end-of-month surprise into a number you watch and act on.

items.title: Prompt caching (Anthropic + OpenAI)
items.body:
## Pay full price for a prompt prefix once, not every time
Many AI features send the same large prefix on every call, a long system prompt, a big set of instructions, a document you are asking questions about. Without caching you pay full input price for those identical tokens every single request. Prompt caching fixes this: the provider stores the processed prefix and, on the next request that starts with the same bytes, serves it from cache at a steep discount (cache reads cost roughly a tenth of normal input tokens). For a feature with a 5,000-token system prompt hit thousands of times a day, caching the prefix is often the single largest cost reduction available.

## The one rule: caching is a prefix match
Everything about caching follows from one invariant: it matches on the exact prefix, so any byte change anywhere in the cached span invalidates everything after it. The practical consequences are concrete. Put your stable content first (the frozen system prompt, the fixed instructions) and your volatile content last (the user's actual question, a timestamp, a request ID), because a `datetime.now()` interpolated into the top of your system prompt changes the prefix every call and silently disables caching entirely. On Anthropic you mark the cacheable boundary explicitly with `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}` on the last stable block; OpenAI caches eligible prefixes automatically. Either way, the design move is the same: freeze the front of your prompt and keep the changing parts at the end.

## Verify it actually cached
Caching fails silently, you get charged full price with no error, so you confirm it from the `usage` data you are already logging. Both providers report cache activity: Anthropic returns `cache_read_input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens`; OpenAI reports cached tokens in its usage details. If `cache_read` stays at zero across repeated calls that should share a prefix, something is invalidating it, almost always a timestamp, an unsorted JSON blob, or a per-request ID sitting in the cached region. The economics have a wrinkle worth knowing: a cache write costs a bit more than a normal token (you pay a small premium to store the prefix), so caching pays off when the prefix is reused enough times to amortise that write, which for a busy feature is immediately. Watch `cache_read` climb on the dashboard and you can see the discount land.

## Where this fits
Add prompt caching to a feature with a large stable prefix (a long system prompt, or a document you query repeatedly), structuring the prompt so the frozen part is first and marked cacheable, then watch the cached-token counts rise and the per-request cost fall on your dashboard. You have pulled the biggest single cost lever, and reinforced the discipline that makes it work: stable content first, volatile content last, verified by the usage numbers.

items.title: Batch APIs
items.body:
## Half price, if you can wait
Not every AI workload needs an answer this second. Generating embeddings for a million documents, classifying a backlog, producing nightly summaries, none of these has a user waiting. For that kind of work both providers offer a Batch API: you submit many requests as one job, the provider processes them asynchronously (within 24 hours, usually much faster), and you pay half the normal token price. For high-volume non-interactive work, that 50% discount is free money you leave on the table by calling the synchronous API in a loop.

## How a batch job works
The shape is the same on both providers: package your requests, submit, poll for completion, collect results.
```python
# Anthropic
batch = client.messages.batches.create(requests=[
    {"custom_id": f"doc-{i}", "params": {"model": "claude-haiku-4-5",
        "max_tokens": 256, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": doc}]}}
    for i, doc in enumerate(docs)
])
# ...later: poll batch.processing_status, then stream results by custom_id
```
The `custom_id` on each request is how you match results back to inputs when they return, because a batch's results are not guaranteed in order. OpenAI's Batch API follows the same submit-poll-retrieve pattern. The tradeoff is explicit and easy to reason about: you give up latency (seconds becomes up-to-hours) and get back 50% of the cost.

## When to batch and when not to
The decision rule is simply whether a human is waiting, the same latency-vs-cost judgement from the rest of the track. Batch the work nobody is watching: bulk embedding, dataset labelling, offline evaluation runs (W17), scheduled report generation. Never batch an interactive request, a user typing in a chat cannot wait an hour for half-price, and using the synchronous API there is correct, not wasteful. The mature pattern in a real product is a split: the interactive path runs synchronously and streams; the heavy background path (re-embedding the corpus, running the nightly eval suite) runs through the Batch API at half cost. Recognising which of your workloads are batchable is a direct, often large line-item saving.

## Where this fits
Identify a non-interactive workload in your projects (embedding a folder of documents is the natural one, and exactly what W9's semantic search needs) and run it through a Batch API, logging the halved cost to your dashboard. You now have the full cost toolkit, measure, cache the stable prefix, route to cheaper models, and batch the non-urgent work, which is everything you need to operate an AI feature affordably at real volume.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
You have a live view of what your AI costs and the levers to control it. By tonight:
- a SQLite-backed cost dashboard shows per-day, per-model, and per-feature spend, plus your ten most expensive requests.
- one of your projects logs every API call's real `usage` and computed cost, tagged by feature.
- your interactive responses stream, with formatted output buffered so it renders cleanly.
- you have applied at least one cost lever, prompt caching, model routing, or batching, and can see its effect on the dashboard.

## The test that proves it
The deliverable is a before-and-after you can point at. Pick one feature, record its per-request cost from the dashboard, apply a lever (cache the system prompt, route simple calls to a smaller model, or move a bulk job to the Batch API), and show the cost drop with the numbers: "caching the system prompt took the invoice parser from $0.011 to $0.002 per call, here's the dashboard before and after." That sentence, a measured cost reduction with the mechanism named, is the exact output of cost engineering, and it is only possible because you instrumented first. A dashboard that shows where the money goes, plus a documented reduction, is worth far more than any claim that your feature is "cheap."

## Ship the artifact
Commit the dashboard, the logging instrumentation, and a short README explaining the cost model (input vs output rates, what's cached, what's batched) and the reduction you achieved. This is an unusually strong portfolio piece, because most engineers who can call an LLM cannot tell you what their feature costs per request or how to halve it. Demonstrating that you measure AI cost, attribute it per feature, and pull the right lever is exactly the operational maturity that distinguishes someone who can build an AI demo from someone who can run an AI product.

## Where this fits in the track
You now control the two levers, speed and cost, that decide whether an AI feature is usable in production, on top of last week's reliability. Streaming and cost instrumentation are not one-week topics; they thread through everything ahead. The agents you build (W13-16) make many model calls per task, so their cost discipline is this week's discipline at higher volume; the production work (W17-20) leans on exactly this measurement layer. Next week you give the model hands, tool use, the mechanism that turns a text generator into something that can act on the world.

weeks.title: Tool Use and Function Calling, Giving LLMs Hands
weeks.context:
Language models are limited to what is in their context window. Tool use is what extends that boundary, it lets the model reach out and touch real systems: your filesystem, a database, an external API, a code executor. The model does not run the tools itself. It decides when to call a tool and with what parameters. Your code runs the tool and returns the result. The model uses the result in its next response. This loop is the foundation of every agent you will build.

This week you build CLI-mate: a terminal chat where the AI has access to filesystem tools. You can ask it to find files that changed today, read their contents, search for patterns, and summarise what it finds. When you run it against one of your earlier roadmap repos, you will see it chain multiple tool calls, list files, read a file, grep for a function, git log, to answer a single question.

Tool schema design is more important than it looks. The model reads the tool name, description, and parameter descriptions to decide whether and how to call each tool. A poorly named tool ("process_query") gives the model nothing. A well-named tool with a precise description and annotated parameters ("list_files: lists files modified within a given time window in a directory. dir: the directory path. modified_within_hours: only include files modified in the last N hours.") gets called correctly.

Side-effect tools, tools that write files, send emails, modify a database, require a different design pattern than read-only tools. The model is not infallible. It will sometimes call a tool with incorrect parameters. For side-effect tools, implement a confirmation pattern: the model proposes the action, your code presents it to the user, the user confirms, then the code executes. This is not a limitation of the protocol, it is how responsible agentic software behaves.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
A language model only knows what is in its context window. Tool use is what breaks that boundary, it lets the model reach out and touch real systems: read a file, query a database, call an API, run code. The crucial mechanic to internalise upfront is that the model does not run anything itself, it decides which tool to call and with what arguments, your code runs the tool and feeds the result back, and the model continues from there. This week you build CLI-mate: a terminal chat where the AI has filesystem tools and can answer real questions about a codebase by chaining calls, list the files changed today, read one, grep for a function, check the git log, all to answer a single question.

## Why this is the most important week before agents
Tool use is the foundation of every agent you will ever build, and this week is where the mechanism stops being abstract. An "agent" is, mechanically, a model in a loop with tools: it calls a tool, sees the result, decides the next call, and repeats until the task is done. Everything in the Agents phase (W13-16), ReAct, planning, multi-step researchers, is variations on the loop you build this week. Get tool use solid now, the schema, the execution loop, the difference between read-only and side-effecting tools, and agents become "the same loop, more tools and a goal" rather than a new and mysterious thing.

## The two mechanics that matter most
Two ideas carry the week. First, tool schema design: the model decides whether and how to call a tool entirely from its name, description, and parameter descriptions, so a vague tool (`process_query`) gets ignored or misused while a precise one (`list_files: list files modified within the last N hours in a directory`) gets called correctly. The tool definition is a prompt, and you write it like one. Second, the execution loop: the model's tool call is a request, not an action; your code executes it and returns the result, and you loop until the model stops asking for tools. Hold those two and tool use is straightforward; miss them and it feels like magic that randomly breaks.

## Where this fits
You build CLI-mate this week, a chat that uses filesystem tools to answer questions about a real repo. It directly extends W6 (a tool call is a schema-constrained structured output) and is the direct prerequisite for the entire Agents phase. This is the week the model stops being a text generator that talks and becomes a system that can act.

items.title: Tool/function calling
items.body:
## The four-step handshake
Tool use is a structured conversation with a fixed shape, and seeing all four steps at once demystifies it. (1) You send the model the user's message plus a list of tool definitions. (2) The model, instead of answering, replies with a tool-use request, the name of a tool and the arguments it wants, which your code receives as structured data, not prose. (3) Your code runs the actual function and gets a result. (4) You send that result back to the model, which uses it to produce its next response (or another tool call). The model never executes anything; it asks, you do it, you report back.

## What a tool definition and a tool call look like
A tool is defined by a name, a description, and a JSON Schema for its parameters, the same `input_schema` shape you used for structured output in W6:
```python
tools = [{
    "name": "read_file",
    "description": "Read and return the full contents of a text file.",
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"path": {"type": "string", "description": "Path to the file"}},
        "required": ["path"],
    },
}]
resp = client.messages.create(model="claude-haiku-4-5", max_tokens=1024,
                              tools=tools, messages=messages)
# resp.stop_reason == "tool_use"; the request is a structured block:
for block in resp.content:
    if block.type == "tool_use":
        result = read_file(**block.input)        # YOU run it
        # then send back a tool_result keyed to block.id
```
The model handed you `block.name` and `block.input` (a dict matching your schema); you call the real function and will return the result keyed to `block.id`.

## The description is the interface the model sees
The single highest-leverage thing in tool use is the quality of the names and descriptions, because they are all the model has to decide with. It cannot see your function body; it reads "Read and return the full contents of a text file" and the `path` description and decides from that. So write tool definitions like prompts: a precise verb-first name, a description that says exactly when to use the tool and what it returns, and a one-line description on every parameter (units, format, constraints). A tool named `process` with no parameter docs is a tool the model will call wrong or not at all; the same capability named and described well gets called correctly on the first try. The recent models reward this especially, they reach for tools more deliberately, so a description that states when to call it noticeably improves the hit rate.

## Where this fits
Define your first filesystem tool (`read_file` or `list_files`) with a precise schema and description, send it to the model, and inspect the tool-use request it returns, the name and the arguments, without executing anything yet. You have seen the request half of the handshake; tomorrow you handle multiple tools at once and wire up the execution that completes the loop.

items.title: Single-tool vs parallel tool calling
items.body:
## The model can ask for several tools at once
Early tool-use mental models assume one call at a time, but modern models do something more efficient: when a task needs several independent pieces of information, the model can request multiple tool calls in a single response. Ask CLI-mate "what changed today and how big are those files," and it may emit two tool-use blocks at once, `list_files(modified_within_hours=24)` and a size lookup, because neither depends on the other. Your response will contain several `tool_use` blocks, and you execute them all and return all their results together before the model continues.

## Handle the list, not just the first block
This changes how you write the execution code: you iterate over every tool-use block in the response, run each, and send back a result for each, matched by id.
```python
results = []
for block in resp.content:
    if block.type == "tool_use":
        output = run_tool(block.name, block.input)      # dispatch by name
        results.append({"type": "tool_result",
                        "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": output})
messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})   # all results in one turn
```
The common beginner bug is handling only `resp.content[0]` and ignoring the rest, which silently drops tool calls and confuses the model. Parallel calls also run faster: independent tools execute concurrently in your code, so two 200ms lookups take 200ms total, not 400ms. (If you ever need to force one-at-a-time, both providers offer a flag to disable parallel calls.)

## Parallel vs sequential is about dependencies
The model parallelises what it can, and the distinction worth understanding is dependency. Independent subtasks, three files to read, two separate lookups, go in parallel because none needs another's result. Dependent subtasks are necessarily sequential: the model must `list_files` before it can `read_file` on one of them, because it does not know the filenames until the first call returns, so those arrive as separate round trips. You do not orchestrate this; the model decides, based on whether one call's arguments depend on another's result. Your job is just to handle however many blocks come back in a given response. Recognising that parallel-where-possible, sequential-where-required pattern is what makes a multi-tool interaction efficient and predictable.

## Where this fits
Extend CLI-mate to handle multiple tool-use blocks per response, executing each and returning all results in one turn, and watch it fire independent lookups in parallel. You now handle the real shape of tool responses, which is the core of the execution loop you formalise in D5, and you have seen how the model naturally splits work into parallel and sequential calls, the seed of agent planning.

items.title: Forced tool use vs auto
items.body:
## Three modes of tool choice
You control how much freedom the model has to use tools, via the `tool_choice` parameter, and the three settings map to three real situations:
- **auto** (the default): the model decides whether to use a tool or just answer in text. This is what you want for a chat assistant, sometimes "what's 2+2" needs no tool, sometimes "what changed today" needs three.
- **any / required**: the model must call some tool (it may pick which), used when a plain text answer is never acceptable.
- **forced** (a specific tool): the model must call the one tool you name, used when you know exactly which action is required.

## When to force, and the W6 connection
The instinct is to leave it on auto, and usually that is right, but forcing has two important uses. The first you already met: in W6 you forced a single "record_invoice" tool to guarantee schema-conforming structured output, the model's only move was to fill in your schema. That is forced tool use as a structured-output trick. The second is control flow: when your application logic knows the next step must be a particular tool (the user clicked "search," so the model must call `search`), forcing removes the chance the model answers from memory instead. The rule of thumb: use auto when the model should decide whether and which tool fits, and force when you have already decided and just want the arguments.

## The cost of over-forcing
Forcing is a sharp tool, and over-using it defeats the point of tool use. If you force a tool on every turn, you have taken away the model's judgement about whether the task needs a tool, so a simple question that deserves a direct answer gets an unnecessary (and sometimes nonsensical) tool call instead. Auto exists because the model is usually good at deciding, and a well-described tool set plus auto handles the mixed reality of real conversations, some turns need tools, some do not. Reserve forcing for the two cases above (guaranteeing structured output, or a step your own logic has already determined); everywhere else, trust auto and invest in good tool descriptions so the model chooses well. Knowing when to constrain the model and when to let it decide is exactly the kind of judgement this track is training.

## Where this fits

items.title: The execution loop
items.body:
## The loop that is the heart of every agent
Up to now you have handled a single round of tool calls; the real pattern is a loop, because the model often needs several rounds to finish a task. CLI-mate answering "find the function that parses dates and show me its tests" needs to: list files, read one, grep for the function, find the test file, read it, then answer, and it discovers each step only after seeing the previous result. The loop that drives this is small and is, almost exactly, what an agent is:
```python
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": question}]
while True:
    resp = client.messages.create(model="claude-haiku-4-5", max_tokens=1024,
                                  tools=tools, messages=messages)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break                                    # model gave a final answer
    results = [run_and_format(b) for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
print(final_text(resp))
```
Each iteration: call the model, run any tools it requested, feed the results back, repeat until it stops asking for tools (`stop_reason` is no longer `tool_use`). That `while` loop is the entire engine.

## Why you build the loop by hand before using a helper
Both SDKs offer a "tool runner" that hides this loop, you register your tool functions and it calls the model, executes tools, and loops for you. Those are convenient and you will use them, but you build the loop by hand first because understanding it is understanding agents. When an agent misbehaves, runs forever, calls the wrong tool, loops on a failure, you debug it by reasoning about this exact loop: what's in `messages`, what the model asked for, what your code returned. An engineer who only knows the magic helper cannot debug the loop; one who has written it can. The helper is an optimisation; the loop is the concept.

## The guardrails a real loop needs
A naive `while True` is a production hazard, and the guardrails are the difference between a tool and a runaway bill. Cap the iterations (`for _ in range(max_steps)`), because a confused model can loop indefinitely, re-calling tools and never concluding, and each iteration is a paid API call. Handle tool errors as results, not crashes: when a tool throws (file not found, bad arguments), return that as the tool result with `is_error: true` so the model can see the failure and adapt, rather than letting an exception kill the loop. And watch the growing `messages` context, every round appends the tool call and its result, so a long loop can balloon the context (and cost) and eventually needs trimming or summarising. These three, a step cap, errors-as-results, and context management, are exactly the concerns that recur, larger, in the Agents phase.

## Where this fits
Wire CLI-mate's full execution loop with a step cap and error handling, and watch it chain several tool calls to answer a real question about your repo. You have built the engine every agent runs on, and the guardrails that keep it safe, which means the Agents phase is now about giving this loop a goal and better tools, not learning a new mechanism.
