items.title: Anthropic computer use vs OpenAI Operator
items.body:
## When the "tool" is a whole computer
Everything so far gave the model tools you wrote, functions with schemas. The frontier extends this idea to its limit: give the model a screen, a mouse, and a keyboard, and let it operate a real graphical computer the way a person does. Anthropic's computer use and OpenAI's computer-using agent (productised as Operator) are the same idea, the model receives a screenshot, decides on an action (click here, type this, scroll), your harness performs it, takes a new screenshot, and the loop repeats. It is the W8 execution loop you just built, with one universal tool, "control the computer", and vision instead of text results. This is how an AI books a flight on a website that has no API, or fills a legacy desktop form: by using the interface a human would.

## Why this is powerful and why it is hard
Computer use unlocks the huge space of systems that have a UI but no clean API, which is most of the software in the world, but it inherits and amplifies every reliability problem of tool use. The model is reading pixels, so it misclicks, misreads a field, or gets lost when a page changes; the loop is long (many screenshot-action rounds), so it is slow and expensive; and the actions are real, a wrong click can submit a form or delete something. It is genuinely impressive and still error-prone, to be used with care, which is exactly why the responsible patterns from this week, confirmation before consequential actions, tight guardrails, matter even more when the action is "click whatever is on screen."

## What to take from this, and the safety line
You will not build a production computer-use agent this week; you need to understand what the category is and where its line sits. The takeaway is conceptual: tool use generalises all the way up to "operate any interface," and the same loop scales from `read_file` to controlling a browser. The safety implication is the sharp part. A read-only tool that lists files is low-stakes; a tool that can click "Buy" or "Send" or "Delete" on a real screen is high-stakes, and an AI that controls a computer can do real damage from a single misread. So the design discipline scales with the stakes: never let an autonomous loop take a consequential, irreversible action without a human in the loop, which is the side-effect-tool confirmation pattern from this week, applied where it matters most.

## Where this fits
Watch a computer-use or Operator demo and map it onto the execution loop you built, screenshot in, action out, repeat, so the connection is concrete rather than magical. You have seen how far tool use extends (to controlling any interface) and why the guardrails get more important as the actions get more powerful, which is exactly the judgement you carry into building real agents next.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
CLI-mate is a terminal chat that can actually do things in your filesystem. By tonight:
- it has a set of well-described filesystem tools (`list_files`, `read_file`, `grep`, `git_log`), each with a precise schema and description.
- it runs the full execution loop, the model chains several tool calls to answer one question, with a step cap and tool errors handled as results.
- read-only tools run freely; any side-effecting tool (writing or deleting a file) goes through a confirmation step before it executes.
- you can point it at a real repo and ask a question that requires several tools, and watch it work.

## The test that proves it
The proof is a multi-step question answered by chained tools, with the chain visible. Ask CLI-mate something that genuinely requires several calls, "which file defines the cost-logging function, and what does its newest test check?", and watch the loop: it lists files, reads or greps to find the function, locates the test, reads it, then answers. Print the tool calls as they happen so the chain is legible. A demo where the AI lists files is trivial; a demo where it composes tools to answer a question it could not answer from any single call is the real capability, and being able to show that chain is the deliverable.

## Ship the artifact
Commit CLI-mate with its tool definitions, the execution loop, the confirmation pattern for side-effecting tools, and a README showing an example multi-tool session. Two things make this a strong portfolio piece. The tool schemas show you understand that a tool definition is a prompt, the names and descriptions are doing the work. And the confirmation pattern on write tools shows you build agentic software responsibly, that you know an LLM will sometimes call a tool wrong and you gate the consequential ones. That judgement, not just the working loop, is what an interviewer probing your agent experience is listening for.

## Where this fits in the track
You have built the loop, model decides, your code acts, results feed back, that every agent runs on, plus the guardrails (step caps, errors-as-results, confirmation on side effects) that keep it safe. That completes the "Building with LLMs" phase: you can now make a model return reliable data (W6), do it fast and affordably (W7), and act on the world through tools (W8). The next phase, RAG and Retrieval, gives the model the other thing it lacks, knowledge beyond its training and its context window, starting with embeddings, the mathematics of meaning. Then the Agents phase combines retrieval and tools into systems that genuinely reason and act.

weeks.title: Embeddings, The Mathematics of Meaning
weeks.context:
Every word, sentence, and paragraph can be represented as a point in a high-dimensional space. Words that mean similar things end up near each other. Sentences with similar intent cluster together. This spatial representation, called an embedding, is what makes semantic search possible: instead of matching keywords, you match meaning.

This week you build a personal semantic search engine over your notes or any folder of markdown files. You walk the directory, split content into paragraphs, embed each paragraph using an embedding API, and store the vectors in SQLite. When you query, you embed the question, compute cosine similarity against every stored vector, and return the top 5 most relevant paragraphs. On 1000 paragraphs, results come back in under 100ms.

The embedding models matter more than most people realise. OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small produces 1536-dimensional vectors and is significantly cheaper than the large variant. Cohere's embed-v4 adds semantic compression. BGE and Nomic models run locally on your laptop with no API call required. The choice affects cost, latency, quality, and whether you need internet connectivity, all relevant tradeoffs for a production system.

Similarity functions are not interchangeable. Cosine similarity measures the angle between vectors and is invariant to magnitude, a good choice when your vectors vary in length. Dot product is equivalent to cosine when vectors are L2-normalised. L2 (Euclidean) distance measures absolute position in space. For most embedding use cases, normalise your vectors and use cosine similarity. The intuition: two documents that express the same idea but one is longer should still be near each other. Cosine handles that; L2 does not.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
Search by keyword finds documents that contain your words. Search by meaning finds documents that express your idea, even in completely different words, and that is what an embedding makes possible. This week you build a personal semantic search engine over your own notes (or any folder of Markdown): you split the files into paragraphs, turn each paragraph into a vector with an embedding model, and store the vectors. When you ask a question, you embed the question too and return the paragraphs whose vectors are closest, the ones that mean the same thing, in well under a tenth of a second over a thousand paragraphs. By Sunday you understand embeddings well enough to build retrieval, the foundation of every RAG system.

## Why this is the start of RAG
A model only knows its training data and what is in its context window, which is why it cannot answer questions about your notes, your company's docs, or anything after its cutoff. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) fixes this by finding the relevant text and putting it in the prompt, and the "finding" is semantic search over embeddings. So this week is the engine of the whole RAG phase: embeddings are how you turn "answer from this corpus the model has never seen" into a tractable problem. Get embeddings and similarity solid now, and vector databases (W10), RAG patterns (W11), and RAG evaluation (W12) are about scaling and refining a retrieval system whose core you built here.

## The one idea: meaning becomes geometry
The mental model that makes embeddings click: an embedding model maps a piece of text to a point in a high-dimensional space, arranged so that things that mean similar things land near each other. "How do I cancel my subscription" and "where do I stop my recurring payment" share almost no words but point to nearly the same place; "cancel" and "Caribbean" share letters but point far apart. Once meaning is geometry, "find the most relevant paragraph" becomes "find the nearest point," a fast, mechanical computation. Everything this week, dimensionality, normalisation, similarity functions, is detail in service of that one idea: text in, a point in space out, closeness equals relatedness.

## Where this fits
You build semantic search over your notes this week. It is the retrieval half of RAG, the thing that finds the right context to feed a model, and it is a genuinely useful tool on its own. Next week you move it from SQLite to a real vector database so it scales past a few thousand vectors; the weeks after add the generation and the evaluation that make it a production RAG system.

items.title: What an embedding actually is
items.body:
## A list of numbers that encodes meaning
Strip away the mystique: an embedding is just a fixed-length list of numbers, a vector, that a model produces for a piece of text. `text-embedding-3-small` turns any text into 1,536 numbers; another model might give you 384 or 1,024. The numbers themselves are not human-readable (no single dimension means "formality" or "topic"), but together they place the text at a specific point in space, and that placement is learned so that semantically similar texts get similar number-lists. You call an API (or a local model) with a string and get back the vector:
```python
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()
v = client.embeddings.create(model="text-embedding-3-small",
                             input="How do I cancel my subscription?").data[0].embedding
len(v)   # 1536  -> a point in 1536-dimensional space
```

## Closeness is the whole point: similarity functions
An embedding alone is inert; the magic is comparing two of them. You measure how close two vectors are, and the standard measure for text is cosine similarity, which compares the angle between two vectors, ignoring their length. Two paragraphs about the same idea point in nearly the same direction (cosine near 1.0) even if one is three times longer; two unrelated paragraphs point in different directions (cosine near 0). That length-invariance is exactly what you want for text, the same idea, stated long or short, should still match, and it is why cosine, not raw Euclidean distance, is the default for embeddings.
```python
import numpy as np
def cosine(a, b):
    a, b = np.array(a), np.array(b)
    return a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))
```

## From two vectors to a search engine
Semantic search is this comparison, repeated. You embed every paragraph in your corpus once and store the vectors. At query time you embed the question, compute its cosine similarity against every stored vector, sort, and return the top few, the paragraphs that mean the most-similar thing to the question. That is the entire algorithm of your search engine: embed-everything-once, then embed-the-query-and-compare. Over a thousand vectors this brute-force compare is fast (milliseconds); the only reason W10 exists is that comparing the query against millions of vectors one by one gets slow, and you need a smarter index. For now, the brute-force version is correct and quick, and it is enough to build a real tool.

## Where this fits
Embed a handful of sentences, compute their pairwise cosine similarities, and confirm the semantically-related ones score high while unrelated ones score low, then extend it to embed every paragraph in a folder of notes and search them. You now have the core of semantic search, text to vector, vector to similarity, similarity to ranked results, which is the retrieval engine the rest of the RAG phase builds on.

items.title: Dimensionality
items.body:
## What the "1536" actually buys you
That an embedding has 1,536 dimensions is not arbitrary, and the number is a real tradeoff. More dimensions give the model more room to encode fine distinctions of meaning, so higher-dimensional embeddings can be more accurate at telling subtly-different texts apart. But every dimension is a number you must store and compute over, so higher dimensions cost more storage (a million 1,536-dim float vectors is gigabytes) and more compute per similarity (every comparison touches every dimension). The dimension count is a quality-versus-cost dial, and like most dials this track teaches, the right setting depends on your scale and your accuracy needs, not on "bigger is better."

## Matryoshka: shorten the vector without re-embedding
A genuinely useful modern feature: some embedding models (including OpenAI's `text-embedding-3` family) are trained so you can truncate the vector to fewer dimensions and keep most of the quality. The important information is packed into the early dimensions, so a 1,536-dim vector cut to 512 still searches well, at a third of the storage and compute. The OpenAI API exposes this directly:
```python
v = client.embeddings.create(model="text-embedding-3-small",
                             input=text, dimensions=512).data[0].embedding  # shorter, cheaper
```
This is a real cost lever for retrieval at scale: if 512 dimensions hits your accuracy bar, you have cut your vector storage and your per-query compute by two-thirds with one parameter. Whether it is worth it is, of course, something you measure (W12).

## Why high-dimensional space is weird, and why it works anyway
A brief intuition that pays off later: high-dimensional space behaves unlike the 2D and 3D space your intuition is built on, distances concentrate, almost everything is "far" from everything else, the so-called curse of dimensionality. This is why exact nearest-neighbour search gets hard at scale and why the approximate index in W10 (HNSW) exists. But it is also why embeddings work: with enough dimensions, the model has the room to place millions of distinct meanings far enough apart to be distinguishable. You do not need the maths, you need the two consequences: dimensions cost resources and can sometimes be trimmed, and high-dimensional geometry is exactly what makes meaning-as-position possible and exact search at scale expensive.

## Where this fits
Compare your search quality and storage at full 1,536 dimensions versus a truncated 512, and feel the cost-quality tradeoff directly on your own notes. You understand what the dimension count costs and buys, and why the move to a real vector database (next week) is partly a response to high-dimensional space making brute-force search expensive as the corpus grows.

items.title: Batch embedding APIs
items.body:
## Embedding a corpus is a bulk job
Searching is one embedding at a time (the query); building the index is thousands or millions of embeddings (the whole corpus), and that bulk step is where cost and time go. The first efficiency is that embedding APIs take many inputs per call: instead of one HTTP request per paragraph, you send a list and get back a list of vectors, which is far faster (one round trip, not a thousand) and the standard way to embed a corpus.
```python
paras = [p for p in all_paragraphs]                  # e.g. 1000 paragraphs
resp = client.embeddings.create(model="text-embedding-3-small", input=paras)  # batched
vectors = [d.embedding for d in resp.data]           # one vector per paragraph
```
There are limits (a maximum number of inputs and total tokens per request), so for a large corpus you chunk the list into batches of a few hundred and loop, but each call still embeds a whole batch at once.

## The Batch API: half price for the bulk pass
For a genuinely large corpus, the W7 lesson returns: embedding a million documents is a non-interactive job nobody is watching, so it belongs on the Batch API at half the cost. You submit all the embedding requests as one batch job, the provider processes them within a few hours, and you pay 50%. This is the canonical batchable workload, the initial index build and any full re-embedding (when you change models or chunking) are exactly the "no human waiting" case where trading latency for half-price is obviously correct. The interactive query path stays synchronous (the user is waiting); the index build runs through batch.

## Embed once, store forever (until you change the model)
The reason batching the build matters so much: you embed each document once and reuse the vector for every future query, so the bulk cost is one-time, not per-search. Store the vectors (in SQLite this week, a vector DB next week) alongside the source text, and queries only ever embed the short question. The one thing that forces a re-embed is changing the embedding model or the chunking, because vectors from different models live in different, incompatible spaces, you cannot compare a `text-embedding-3-small` vector to a vector from another model. So the practical rule is: pick your embedding model deliberately, embed the corpus once (cheaply, via batch), and budget for a full re-embed only when you intentionally switch models. That one-time-build, many-queries economics is what makes semantic search affordable.

## Where this fits
Embed your whole notes corpus with batched calls (and, if it is large, via the Batch API), store the vectors with their source text, and confirm queries now only embed the short question. You have the efficient build pipeline for a retrieval index, embed-the-corpus-once-cheaply, query-against-it-forever, which is the cost structure that makes RAG over a large corpus practical.

items.title: Normalisation
items.body:
## Make every vector the same length
Recall from D2 that cosine similarity compares the angle between vectors and ignores their magnitude. Normalisation is the trick that makes this cheap and consistent: you scale every vector to unit length (L2 norm = 1) so they all sit on the same sphere, differing only in direction. Once every stored vector and every query vector is normalised, the geometry is purely about direction, which is exactly what you want for "same meaning regardless of length."
```python
import numpy as np
def normalise(v):
    v = np.array(v)
    return v / np.linalg.norm(v)     # now ||v|| == 1
```
Some embedding APIs return already-normalised vectors; many do not, so normalising on the way into your store is a safe default.

## Why normalisation makes the dot product equal cosine
The payoff is a real performance win, and it is worth understanding the small piece of maths because it explains a setting you will see in every vector database. Cosine similarity divides the dot product by both vectors' magnitudes; if both vectors are already unit-length, those magnitudes are 1, so cosine similarity collapses to a plain dot product. The dot product is a single fast multiply-and-sum with no division, which matters enormously when you are doing it millions of times. So the standard production setup is: normalise all vectors once at storage time, then use dot product as your similarity, getting cosine's length-invariance at the dot product's speed. This is why vector databases ask you to pick a "distance metric" and why "cosine" and "dot product on normalised vectors" are the same choice.

## The consistency rule that prevents silent bugs
The one discipline normalisation demands: be consistent. If you normalise your stored vectors, you must normalise your query vector too, comparing a normalised vector to an un-normalised one gives meaningless similarities and silently-wrong results (no error, just bad rankings). The same applies to the distance metric: the metric you index with must match the metric you query with. These are the kind of silent retrieval bugs that are maddening to debug because nothing crashes, the search just returns subtly worse results, so the rule is to normalise everything at the boundary (both corpus and query) and pick one metric for the whole system. Consistency in, consistency out.

## Where this fits
Normalise all your stored vectors and your query vector, switch your similarity from cosine to dot product, and confirm the rankings are identical but the search is faster. You understand the normalise-then-dot-product setup every vector database uses, and the consistency rule that keeps semantic search correct, which is exactly the configuration you will choose when you move to a real vector DB next week.

items.title: Open-source embedding models you can run on your laptop (Sentence Transformers)
items.body:
## You don't always need an API
Every embedding so far went to an API, which means cost, latency, and an internet dependency. For a lot of use cases you need none of that: strong open-source embedding models run on your own laptop, for free, with no API call. The `sentence-transformers` library is the standard way to use them, and it is two lines:
```python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
model = SentenceTransformer("BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5")   # downloads once, runs locally
vectors = model.encode(paragraphs, normalize_embeddings=True)   # numpy array, no API
```
Models like BGE and Nomic are competitive with the commercial APIs on quality for many tasks, and they embed text entirely on your machine, so the marginal cost of embedding a million paragraphs is electricity, not dollars.

## The real tradeoff: API vs local
This is a genuine engineering decision with clear axes, and naming them is the lesson:
- **Cost:** local models are free to run (no per-token charge); APIs charge per token, which adds up on a large or frequently-re-embedded corpus.
- **Privacy:** local embedding never sends your data anywhere, which can be decisive for sensitive documents (medical, legal, internal code).
- **Latency and connectivity:** local has no network round trip and works offline; an API needs connectivity and adds a hop.
- **Operational simplicity:** an API is zero-ops (someone else runs the model); local means you manage the model, the hardware, and getting a GPU if you want speed at scale.
The commercial APIs buy you convenience and often a quality edge; local models buy you cost, privacy, and independence.

## When to reach for which
The decision rule follows the axes. Reach for a local model when cost at scale matters, when the data is sensitive and must not leave your infrastructure, or when you need offline operation, embedding a huge private corpus is the textbook case. Reach for an API when you want zero operational burden, the absolute best quality, or you are embedding low enough volume that the cost is trivial. Many production systems use both: a local model for the bulk corpus embedding (cheap, private) and sometimes an API for a quality-sensitive path. The meta-point is the same judgement the whole track trains, there is no universally right embedding model, only the right one for your cost, privacy, and quality constraints, and an AI engineer is expected to reason about that tradeoff rather than reflexively reach for the API.

## Where this fits
Swap your notes search from the OpenAI API to a local `sentence-transformers` model, confirm it works offline with no per-call cost, and compare the result quality. You can now build semantic search with or without an API, and reason about which fits a given system's cost and privacy needs, which is the kind of platform decision you will defend when you design real retrieval systems.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
A working semantic search engine over your own notes. By tonight:
- you embed a folder of Markdown into vectors (via API or a local model) and store them with their source paragraphs.
- a query embeds the question, computes similarity against every stored vector, and returns the top few most-relevant paragraphs, fast.
- you understand and can defend your choices: which embedding model, how many dimensions, normalised with which similarity metric.
- you can find a note by its meaning even when it shares no keywords with your query.

## The test that proves it
The deliverable is a query that keyword search would miss. Search your notes for an idea using words that do NOT appear in the relevant note, "how to stay focused" when the note actually says "techniques for avoiding distraction", and watch semantic search surface it anyway. That is the whole point made concrete: you matched meaning, not strings, which `grep` could never do. Then sanity-check the ranking on a few queries you know the answer to, the right paragraph should be in the top few. A search engine that finds the right note by meaning, demonstrated on a query with no shared keywords, is the proof that embeddings work and that you built retrieval correctly.

## Ship the artifact
Commit the search engine with its embedding pipeline, the similarity search, and a README stating your choices and their reasons (model, dimensions, metric) and showing an example meaning-based query. The portfolio signal is that you understand retrieval from first principles, text to vector, vector to ranked results, not as a black box but as something you can build, tune, and explain. Most people who use RAG cannot tell you what an embedding is or why cosine; demonstrating the engine yourself shows you can build and reason about the retrieval layer every RAG system depends on.

## Where this fits in the track
You have built the retrieval engine, semantic search over a corpus, that is the heart of RAG. It works beautifully up to a few thousand vectors with brute-force comparison. The moment you have millions of vectors, comparing the query against every one becomes too slow, and you need specialised indexing and a real database, which is exactly next week (Vector Databases): the same retrieval, scaled, with the approximate-nearest-neighbour index and the hybrid search that production systems use. After that you add the generation (RAG patterns) and the evaluation that turn retrieval into a trustworthy answer system.

weeks.title: Vector Databases, Where Your Embeddings Actually Live
weeks.context:
Storing embeddings in SQLite works for thousands of vectors. It breaks for millions. The vector database landscape exists because similarity search at scale requires specialised indexing, algorithms that avoid comparing every query vector against every stored vector. This week you build a hybrid search API: FastAPI endpoint, Qdrant or pgvector for storage, BM25 keyword search combined with vector search, and a cross-encoder reranker on the merged results.

The landscape of vector databases is genuinely diverse and the differences matter. pgvector is an extension to PostgreSQL, it gives you vector search in a database you already know, with all of PostgreSQL's transactional guarantees and the ability to join against regular tables. Pinecone is a managed vector-only service, operationally simple, expensive at scale. Qdrant, Weaviate, and Milvus are dedicated vector databases with more indexing options than pgvector. LanceDB uses a columnar format that works well for multi-modal data. The right choice depends on your existing infrastructure, scale, and whether you need transactions.

HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is the indexing algorithm behind most modern vector databases. It builds a layered graph of connections between vectors, allowing approximate nearest-neighbor search in O(log n) time instead of O(n). The tradeoff: approximate, not exact. For most retrieval tasks, the approximation loss is negligible, but understanding it matters when you are evaluating recall metrics.

Hybrid search is the pattern that real search systems use. Vector search alone misses documents with specific terminology. Keyword search alone misses semantically similar documents with different vocabulary. Combining both via reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) consistently outperforms either alone. The cross-encoder reranker then takes the combined top-50 and reorders them by a more expensive but more precise relevance model. Two-stage retrieval is the standard architecture.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
Your SQLite semantic search from W9 works, and it has a ceiling: brute-force comparison against every vector is fine for a few thousand and falls over at a few million. This week you move retrieval to a real vector database and make it production-grade. You build a hybrid search API: a FastAPI endpoint backed by a real vector store (Qdrant or pgvector), combining keyword search and vector search, with a reranker that reorders the results by a more precise relevance model. By Sunday you have the two-stage retrieval architecture that actual search systems run on, not a toy, the thing you would put behind a product's search bar.

## Why brute force breaks, and what replaces it
The core problem a vector database solves is one of scale. Comparing a query vector against N stored vectors one by one is O(N), fine at a thousand, unacceptable at ten million (every search would scan the whole corpus). Vector databases use approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) indexes that find the closest vectors in roughly O(log N) by being willing to be approximately right, occasionally missing a true nearest neighbour in exchange for being hundreds of times faster. That tradeoff, a tiny, usually-negligible accuracy loss for an enormous speed gain, is the entire reason the vector-database category exists, and understanding it is what lets you reason about search recall later.

## The two upgrades that make search actually good
Beyond scale, this week adds the two techniques that separate real search from naive vector search. Hybrid search combines vector search (great at meaning, bad at exact terms like a product code or a name) with keyword search (the opposite), because each covers the other's blind spot, and combining them beats either alone. Reranking is a second, more precise pass: cheap retrieval pulls a broad candidate set, then an expensive, accurate model reorders just those candidates, so you get both speed and precision. This two-stage retrieval (fast broad recall, then precise rerank) is the standard architecture, and building it is what turns "I can do vector search" into "I can build a search system."

## Where this fits
You move your retrieval to a real vector database and add hybrid search and reranking this week. It is W9's engine, scaled and refined into production shape. Next week (RAG Patterns) you feed these retrieved results to a model to generate answers, and the week after you learn to evaluate the whole pipeline, but a RAG system is only as good as its retrieval, so this week's quality work is what everything downstream depends on.

items.title: Vector DB landscape
items.body:
## The choice that actually depends on your existing stack
There are many vector databases, and the differences are real, but the decision is less about benchmarks than about your situation. The landscape, with the axis that matters for each:
- **pgvector** is a PostgreSQL extension, vector search inside the database you probably already run, with real transactions and the ability to JOIN vectors against your normal tables. The default when you already have Postgres and do not want another system.
- **Pinecone** is a fully-managed, vector-only service, operationally simple (someone else runs it), and expensive at scale. The default when you want zero ops and will pay for it.
- **Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus** are dedicated vector databases with richer indexing and filtering options than pgvector, the default when vector search is central and you have outgrown an extension.
- **LanceDB** uses a columnar on-disk format that suits multimodal and larger-than-memory data.

## The decision rule, not the benchmark
The mistake is choosing on a feature-comparison table; the right move is choosing on your constraints, the same lesson as picking a cloud or a database anywhere. Three questions usually decide it. What do you already run? If you have Postgres, pgvector means no new system to operate, often decisive for a small team. What is your scale? A few hundred thousand vectors run fine in pgvector; hundreds of millions push you toward a dedicated store built for that. Do you need transactions and joins? If your vectors must stay consistent with relational data (delete a user, delete their vectors atomically; filter by a column you JOIN to), pgvector's database guarantees are worth a lot; a vector-only store makes that harder. Answer those and the choice usually falls out, no benchmark required.

## Start boring, scale deliberately
The pragmatic default mirrors the cloud-choice lesson from other tracks: start with the simplest thing that fits your stack and scale only when you must. For most teams that means pgvector (you keep one database, get transactions and joins, and avoid operating a second system) until your scale or feature needs genuinely outgrow it, at which point a dedicated vector database earns its operational cost. Reaching for a specialised vector database on day one, when pgvector would serve a hundred-thousand-vector corpus comfortably, is the same over-engineering this track keeps warning against. Pick the boring option that fits, and let real scale, not anticipated scale, drive you to something more specialised.

## Where this fits
Choose a vector database for your hybrid search API (pgvector if you want one system, Qdrant if you want dedicated vector features) and reason explicitly about why, on stack, scale, and transactions. You can now make the storage decision deliberately, which is the foundation under the hybrid search and reranking you build the rest of the week, and a real architectural call you will defend in any RAG design discussion.

items.title: Hybrid search
items.body:
## Two kinds of search, opposite blind spots
Vector search and keyword search fail in exactly complementary ways, which is why combining them wins. Vector search matches meaning, so it finds "techniques for avoiding distraction" when you search "how to focus", but it is weak on exact terms: a specific product code, an error string, a person's name, an acronym, can get fuzzed into something semantically near but wrong. Keyword search (the classic BM25 algorithm) is the mirror image: it nails exact terms and is useless when the document uses different words for the same idea. Each alone misses a whole class of relevant results; hybrid search runs both and merges them, covering both blind spots.

## Reciprocal Rank Fusion: merging two ranked lists
The problem with combining two searches is that their scores are not comparable, a cosine similarity of 0.82 and a BM25 score of 14.3 are on different scales. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) sidesteps this elegantly by combining ranks instead of scores: each document gets a score based on its position in each list, 1/(k + rank), and the combined ranking sums those across both searches. A document that ranks highly in either search rises; one that ranks well in both rises most.
```python
def rrf(rankings, k=60):                 # rankings: list of ranked id-lists
    scores = {}
    for ranked in rankings:
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(ranked):
            scores[doc_id] = scores.get(doc_id, 0) + 1 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)
```
RRF is simple, needs no score tuning, and consistently beats either search alone, which is why it is the standard fusion method.

## The reranker: a precise second pass
Hybrid search gives you a good candidate set; a cross-encoder reranker makes the top of it excellent. The retrieval models so far are bi-encoders: they embed query and document separately, which is fast (you can pre-compute document vectors) but loses some precision. A cross-encoder reads the query and a document together and scores their relevance directly, which is far more accurate and far too slow to run over the whole corpus. So you use it as a second stage: hybrid search cheaply retrieves the top ~50 candidates, then the cross-encoder reranks just those 50 and you keep the top few. This two-stage retrieval, fast broad recall, then precise rerank, gets you the speed of vector search and the accuracy of a heavy relevance model, and it is the architecture real search systems use.

## Where this fits
Build the full pipeline: BM25 keyword search plus vector search, merged with RRF, then a cross-encoder reranker over the merged top-50. Run it against your corpus and compare it to plain vector search, the hybrid-plus-rerank results should be visibly better, especially on queries with specific terms. You have built production-grade retrieval, the two-stage architecture that makes RAG answers trustworthy, which is exactly the quality the generation and evaluation weeks depend on.

items.title: Multi-tenancy
items.body:
## Many users, one search system, strict isolation
A real search product serves many users (or teams, or customers), and each must only ever see their own data, user A's query must never return user B's documents. That is multi-tenancy, and getting it right is a correctness-and-privacy requirement, not a nice-to-have: a retrieval system that leaks one tenant's documents into another's results is a data breach. The core mechanism is metadata filtering: you store a `tenant_id` (or `user_id`) alongside every vector, and every query filters to the current tenant's vectors before or during the similarity search, so the search space is structurally scoped to the right owner.
```python
# every vector carries its owner; every query is filtered to that owner
results = client.search(collection="docs", query_vector=qv,
    query_filter={"must": [{"key": "tenant_id", "match": {"value": current_user}}]},
    limit=10)
```

## Filtering must happen with the search, not after it
The subtle, important part: the filter has to be applied as part of the indexed search, not by fetching results and discarding the wrong-tenant ones afterward. Post-filtering, search globally then drop other tenants' hits, is both a privacy risk (the data was retrieved) and broken (you ask for the top 10 and might get 10 results that all belong to other tenants, leaving you nothing for the right one). Good vector databases support filtered search that restricts the ANN traversal to matching vectors, so the index only ever considers the current tenant's data. This is exactly why the earlier point about transactions and filtering matters when choosing a database: native, efficient metadata filtering is a real differentiator, and a store that can only post-filter is unsafe for multi-tenant use.

## Isolation models, from shared to separate
There is a spectrum of how strongly you isolate tenants, trading simplicity against strength, the same soft-vs-hard boundary idea from infrastructure. A shared collection with a tenant filter (above) is simplest and fine for many tenants who trust the platform, one index, scoped by metadata. Separate collections (or namespaces) per tenant isolate more strongly and can perform better per-tenant, at more operational overhead. Separate databases per tenant is the strongest isolation, for high-security or per-customer-compliance cases, and the most expensive to run. The right level depends on your trust and compliance requirements, and the engineering judgement is to use the lightest isolation that actually meets them, not to reflexively spin up a database per user.

## Where this fits
Add a `tenant_id` to every vector and a tenant filter to every query in your search API, and prove that one tenant's query cannot return another's documents. You have made your retrieval system safe to serve multiple users, which is a hard requirement for any real product and a common source of serious bugs, and you understand the isolation spectrum so you can match it to a system's actual security needs.

items.title: Sharding and scale
items.body:
## What "at scale" actually breaks
Retrieval that works at a million vectors meets new problems at a hundred million, and knowing what breaks first is the point. The two pressures are memory and throughput. ANN indexes like HNSW are fast because they hold the graph in RAM, so a corpus whose vectors exceed one machine's memory cannot be served from a single node, that is the wall you hit first. And a single node can only handle so many queries per second, so high traffic needs more serving capacity. The answer to both is sharding: split the vectors across multiple nodes, so each holds a fraction of the index in its memory, and queries fan out across them.

## How sharded search works
Sharding a vector index has a shape worth understanding because it explains the cost. You partition the corpus across N shards (by hash, or by tenant, or by some key), and each shard holds its slice of the index in memory. A query goes to all shards, each returns its local top-k, and a coordinator merges those partial results into a global top-k. This scatter-gather means you can serve a corpus far larger than one machine's RAM and more queries by adding nodes, but it adds coordination overhead (every query touches every shard) and operational complexity (more nodes to run, rebalance, and keep healthy). It is the same scale-out pattern as a sharded database, applied to vectors.

## You probably don't need this yet
The honest framing, consistent with the whole track: sharding is a real technique you should understand and almost certainly do not need at your scale. A single well-configured node handles millions of vectors comfortably, and managed services (Pinecone, cloud Qdrant) handle the sharding for you when you do cross that line, so you rarely operate it by hand. The value of this lesson is recognition: knowing that vector search scales by sharding, what that costs (memory per node, coordination per query, ops per cluster), and that "we need to shard" is a decision driven by measured memory and throughput limits, not anticipated ones. Reaching for a sharded cluster before you have outgrown one node is the same premature-scaling mistake the track keeps flagging, the right move is to run the simplest thing until the metrics force you to scale out, then let a managed service do it where you can.

## Where this fits
Reason through how your search system would scale past one machine, what runs out first (memory for the index), how sharding spreads the load, and why a managed service usually handles it for you. You understand the scaling story for retrieval, which lets you design a system that can grow and recognise when it actually needs to, without over-building a distributed cluster for a corpus a single node would serve.

items.title: Migrating between vector DBs
items.body:
## Why you'll eventually move
The vector database you pick on day one is rarely the one you run forever: you start on pgvector and outgrow it, you are on an expensive managed service and want to cut cost, your scale or feature needs change. So migrating between vector databases is a real operational task, and the reason it is worth a lesson is that it is both more annoying and less scary than it first looks. More annoying because there is no universal export format and each database has its own API and index config; less scary because the expensive part, the embeddings themselves, is reusable.

## The vectors are portable; the index is not
The key insight that makes migration tractable: an embedding is just a list of numbers, and those numbers do not change between databases. A `text-embedding-3-small` vector is the same 1,536 floats whether it lives in pgvector, Qdrant, or Pinecone, so you do NOT re-embed your corpus to migrate (which would be the costly part), you export the existing vectors and their metadata and bulk-load them into the new store, then rebuild the index (the HNSW graph) there. What is database-specific is the index structure and the query API, not the data. So a migration is: export (id, vector, metadata, source text) from the old store, import into the new one, let it build its index, and point your query code at the new API.
```text
old DB  --export-->  [ {id, vector:[...1536], metadata, text}, ... ]  --import-->  new DB  (builds its own index)
```

## The two things to get right
Migrations go wrong in predictable places, and naming them is the practical content. First, the distance metric and normalisation must match, if the old store used cosine on normalised vectors, the new one must too, or your rankings silently change (the consistency rule from W9, at the system level). Second, do not cut over blindly: run the new store in parallel, compare its results to the old store on a set of test queries (the evaluation habit from W6, and W12 ahead), and only switch traffic once the new system returns equivalent results. The fact that vectors are portable is what makes this safe, you can stand up the new database with the exact same data and verify it matches before trusting it, rather than re-embedding and hoping. A migration you have validated against the old system's results is a migration you can ship.

## Where this fits
Export your vectors and metadata from this week's store and load them into a different one (pgvector to Qdrant, or vice versa), keeping the metric consistent, and verify the two return matching results on test queries. You can now move a retrieval system between databases without re-embedding and without breaking it, which is exactly the operational flexibility that lets you choose a store for today without locking yourself in forever.

## What you ship this week
A production-shaped hybrid search API. By tonight:
- a FastAPI endpoint backed by a real vector database (Qdrant or pgvector), not SQLite.
- hybrid retrieval, BM25 keyword search and vector search merged with RRF, followed by a cross-encoder reranker over the merged candidates.
- multi-tenant isolation, every vector tagged by owner, every query filtered, so no tenant can see another's data.
- a deliberate, defensible choice of database, with the reasoning (stack, scale, transactions) written down.

## The test that proves it
The proof is a query that breaks plain vector search but the hybrid system handles. Search for something with a specific term, a product code, an error string, an exact name, where pure semantic search drifts to something merely related; hybrid search (keyword catching the exact term, vector catching the meaning, RRF merging, reranker sharpening) returns the right document. Show the difference: the same query through plain vector search versus the full pipeline, side by side. And prove the isolation: a query as tenant A never returns tenant B's documents. "Plain vector search missed the exact part number; hybrid plus rerank found it, and tenant filtering keeps results scoped, here are both" is the deliverable, a measurably better, safely-isolated retrieval system.

## Ship the artifact
Commit the search API with its vector store, the hybrid + RRF + reranker pipeline, the tenant filtering, and a README explaining the architecture and the database choice. This is a strong portfolio piece because two-stage hybrid retrieval is exactly what real search and RAG systems run, and most people who "do RAG" stop at naive vector search. Demonstrating hybrid search, a reranker, and multi-tenant isolation on a real vector database shows you can build the retrieval layer of a production AI system, not just a demo that works on a clean corpus.

## Where this fits in the track
You now have production-grade retrieval, scaled to a real database, made accurate with hybrid search and reranking, and made safe with tenant isolation. That completes the retrieval half of RAG. Next week (RAG Patterns) you connect it to generation: feed these retrieved results to a model to produce grounded answers, and learn the patterns (and failure modes, like the model ignoring the context or hallucinating anyway) that separate naive RAG from a system that actually answers correctly. Then W12 teaches you to measure whether your RAG is any good, because, as always on this track, an answer system you cannot evaluate is one you cannot trust.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have 50k documents indexed in Qdrant with HNSW. Your exact nearest-neighbor search (brute force) takes 800ms. HNSW takes 15ms but returns slightly different results. You set ef (the search parameter) higher to improve recall and the query time goes to 45ms. What is ef and what does it control? ef (ef_search in Qdrant) is the size of the candidate set during graph traversal. Higher ef means the algorithm explores more nodes before returning results, improving recall at the cost of latency. The relationship is not linear, doubling ef does not double latency. Tune ef by measuring recall@10 against brute force at different ef values and choosing the lowest ef that achieves your recall target (typically 0.95+).

weeks.title: RAG Patterns, Beyond Naive Retrieval
weeks.context:
Naive RAG is simple: chunk documents, embed them, retrieve the top-k by similarity, stuff them into the prompt. It works on demos. In production, it fails in specific and predictable ways: the user asks a multi-part question and the retrieval only captures part of it; the user uses different vocabulary than the document; the retrieved chunks lack the context needed to understand them in isolation. This week you go beyond naive retrieval and build a paper assistant that implements the patterns that address each of these failures.

Query rewriting is the first pattern. The user's query is rarely the ideal retrieval query. HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings) generates a hypothetical answer to the question, then embeds and retrieves that hypothetical answer against the corpus, because what a correct answer looks like is often closer to relevant documents than what the question looks like. Multi-query generates multiple different phrasings of the question and retrieves for each, then merges and deduplicates the result sets.

Contextual chunk headers address the isolated chunk problem. A paragraph that says "The third limitation is..." is meaningless without knowing what is being limited. Prepending the document title, section heading, and a one-sentence summary before each chunk's embedding ensures the model retrieving it has context about where it came from.

The retrieval-then-rerank pipeline applies the cross-encoder pattern from last week at this level: retrieve a large candidate set (top-50 or top-100) with fast approximate search, then rerank the candidates with a more expensive model that scores (query, passage) pairs jointly. The reranker consistently improves the final top-5 by catching relevant documents that were ranked poorly by vector similarity alone.

Building on ArXiv papers forces you to work with real documents that have structure: abstract, introduction, methodology, results, conclusion. Your chunking and retrieval strategy must account for that structure.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
Naive RAG, chunk, embed, retrieve top-k, stuff into the prompt, works in a demo and fails in production in predictable ways. This week you build a paper assistant over real ArXiv papers and fix those failures one pattern at a time. The patterns address concrete problems: the user's question is a bad retrieval query (so you rewrite it), a retrieved chunk is meaningless out of context (so you give chunks context), the top result by vector similarity is not actually the most relevant (so you rerank), and the model's answer is not grounded in the sources (so you cite). By Sunday your RAG is not "retrieve and pray", it is a pipeline whose every stage you can name, justify, and improve.

## Why naive RAG fails, specifically
The failures are not random, they are structural, and naming them is the week's spine:
- **Query-document mismatch:** the user asks "why doesn't this scale" but the paper says "computational complexity"; the question and the answer use different words, so similarity search misses.
- **Lost context:** a chunk that reads "The third limitation is..." is meaningless retrieved alone, you do not know what is being limited or where it came from.
- **Imperfect ranking:** vector similarity is a fast approximation of relevance, so the genuinely best passage is sometimes ranked 8th, not 1st.
- **Ungrounded answers:** the model gets good context and still hallucinates, or answers without pointing at the source, so you cannot trust or verify it.
Each pattern this week targets one of these, which is why "beyond naive RAG" is a set of specific fixes, not a vibe.

## The mindset: RAG is a pipeline you tune, not a black box
The shift from naive RAG to production RAG is treating retrieval as an engineered pipeline with stages you measure and improve, not a single magic step. Chunk the documents thoughtfully, optionally rewrite the query, retrieve a broad candidate set, rerank it precisely, give the model well-contextualised chunks, and make it cite. Every stage has knobs (chunk size, how many candidates, which reranker) and every knob is a quality-or-cost decision you make deliberately. Working on real ArXiv papers forces this, because real documents have structure (abstract, methods, results) and messy formatting that a clean demo corpus hides. That pipeline-tuning mindset is what separates someone who "used a RAG library" from someone who can make RAG actually work.

## Where this fits
You build the paper assistant this week, layering the patterns that fix naive RAG's failures, on top of the retrieval engine from W9-10. It is the generation-and-quality half of RAG. But notice the recurring problem: every pattern claims to "improve" retrieval, and you have no way to know if it actually did, which is exactly why next week is RAG Evaluation. You cannot tune a pipeline you cannot measure, so this week ends pointing straight at the metrics that tell you whether your clever pattern helped or hurt.

items.title: Chunking strategies
items.body:
## Chunking is the decision that quietly determines everything
Before retrieval can be good, the chunks have to be good, and chunking is the most under-appreciated lever in RAG. You cannot embed a whole 30-page paper as one vector (you would retrieve all of it or none), so you split it into pieces, and how you split decides what retrieval can ever find. Chunk too small (a sentence) and each piece lacks the context to be meaningful or to answer anything; chunk too large (a whole section) and a chunk covers many ideas, so its single embedding is a blurry average and retrieval gets imprecise. The whole game is finding chunks big enough to be self-contained and small enough to be about one thing.

## The strategies, from naive to structure-aware
There is a ladder of chunking approaches, and matching it to your documents is the skill:
- **Fixed-size** (e.g. 500 tokens with a 50-token overlap) is the simple default, the overlap stops an idea from being split exactly at a boundary. Fine for uniform prose.
- **Recursive/semantic** splits on natural boundaries (paragraphs, then sentences) so chunks align with meaning rather than an arbitrary token count.
- **Structure-aware** uses the document's own structure, and this is what real documents demand. An ArXiv paper has sections (abstract, methods, results); chunking along those boundaries keeps each chunk topically coherent, where a fixed-size split would cheerfully merge the end of "methods" with the start of "results" into one incoherent chunk.
The lesson of working on real papers is that structure-aware chunking beats fixed-size precisely because real documents have structure to exploit.

## The overlap-and-coherence tradeoff
Two design parameters carry most of the quality. Overlap: chunks that share a little text at their edges prevent an answer that straddles a boundary from being lost (the key sentence is not cut in half), at the cost of some duplication and storage. Coherence: a chunk should be about one retrievable thing, because its embedding represents the whole chunk, so a chunk spanning two topics has a muddy vector that matches neither well. The discipline is to chunk so each piece is a coherent, self-contained unit of meaning, with enough overlap that nothing important falls in a crack. Get chunking wrong and no amount of clever reranking saves you, because the right answer was never in a retrievable chunk to begin with, which is why this comes first.

## Where this fits
Implement structure-aware chunking for your ArXiv papers, splitting along sections with sensible size and overlap, and compare retrieval against a naive fixed-size split. You have fixed the foundation, good chunks are the precondition for everything downstream, and set up the retrieval-and-rerank pipeline that operates on them next.

items.title: Retrieval-then-rerank pipeline
items.body:
## The two-stage pattern, at the RAG level
You met retrieve-then-rerank in W10 for search; here it is the spine of RAG generation, and it is worth restating because it is the single highest-leverage quality pattern. Stage one: retrieve broadly and cheaply, pull a large candidate set (top-50 or top-100) with fast vector (or hybrid) search, optimising for recall, getting all the possibly-relevant chunks into the candidate pool even if their order is rough. Stage two: rerank precisely and expensively, run a cross-encoder over just those candidates to score each (query, chunk) pair jointly, and keep the top 5 for the prompt. Cheap-and-broad then expensive-and-sharp gives you both recall and precision, which neither stage alone provides.

## Why retrieve more than you keep
The non-obvious move that makes this work: retrieve far more candidates than you will actually use. If you want 5 chunks in the prompt, you do not retrieve 5, you retrieve 50 and rerank down to 5. The reason is that vector similarity is an approximate relevance signal, so the genuinely-best chunk is often not in the vector top-5 but is in the vector top-50; a wider net at stage one gives the reranker a chance to find it. Retrieving exactly k and stopping bakes in vector search's ranking errors; retrieving 10k candidates and reranking lets a more accurate model correct them. The candidate-set size is a knob: bigger means better recall and a slower, costlier rerank, so you tune it against your quality and latency needs.

## Why the reranker is worth its cost
The reranker is more expensive per item than vector search, so why pay it? Because it reads the query and the chunk together and judges actual relevance, where the bi-encoder embedded them separately and only compared directions. That joint reading catches the cases vector similarity gets wrong: a chunk that is topically near but does not actually answer the question gets demoted; a chunk that answers it in different words gets promoted. The result is a consistently better final top-5, the chunks that actually go into the model's prompt, which directly determines answer quality (the model can only ground its answer in what you retrieve). You only run the expensive reranker over ~50 candidates, not the whole corpus, so the cost is bounded and the precision gain is large, which is exactly why two-stage retrieval is the production standard.

## Where this fits
Build the retrieve-50-then-rerank-to-5 pipeline into your paper assistant, and compare the final chunks (and the answers they produce) against naive top-5 vector retrieval. You have added the highest-leverage quality stage, which directly improves the context the model answers from, and reinforced the pattern, cheap broad recall then expensive precise rerank, that recurs across every retrieval system you will build.

days.title: Late chunking and contextual retrieval
days.summary: Focus: Late chunking and contextual retrieval

items.title: Late chunking and contextual retrieval
items.body:
## The isolated-chunk problem, stated sharply
A chunk has to be embedded as a standalone piece, but its meaning often depends on context it no longer carries. "The third limitation is the quadratic memory cost" is a great sentence in a paper and a terrible chunk in isolation: retrieved alone, the embedding does not know what has a third limitation, which method, which paper. So the chunk's vector under-represents what it is actually about, and retrieval for "memory problems in transformers" misses it even though it is exactly relevant. Two modern techniques fix this by restoring the context the chunk lost, and both noticeably improve retrieval on real documents.

## Contextual retrieval: prepend the context before embedding
The first fix, popularised by Anthropic as contextual retrieval, is direct: before embedding each chunk, prepend a short, chunk-specific blurb of context, the document title, the section it is from, and a one-sentence summary of what surrounds it, often generated by a cheap LLM call per chunk. So "The third limitation is the quadratic memory cost" gets embedded as "[From 'Efficient Transformers', Limitations section, discussing the model's scaling drawbacks] The third limitation is the quadratic memory cost." Now the embedding carries the context, and a query about transformer memory finds it. You store the original chunk for the prompt but embed the context-enriched version, the context improves retrieval without bloating what the model reads.

## Late chunking: embed the whole document, then split
The second fix, late chunking, attacks the same problem from the other end. Instead of splitting first and embedding each isolated piece, you run the whole document (or a large window) through the embedding model first, so every token's representation is informed by the surrounding document, then pool those contextualised token representations into per-chunk vectors. The effect is that each chunk's embedding "remembers" the document context it came from, because it was computed while the model could still see the neighbours, rather than after they were cut away. It needs an embedding model that exposes token-level outputs and a long enough context window, but where it applies it gives chunks document-aware vectors for free, no extra LLM calls.

## Where this fits
Add contextual retrieval (prepend title + section + summary before embedding) to your paper assistant, and understand late chunking as the alternative approach, then measure whether retrieval on context-dependent chunks improves. You have fixed the isolated-chunk failure, one of naive RAG's worst, which matters most exactly on the structured, cross-referential documents (like papers) that real RAG has to handle, and you have seen two different angles on the same core problem: a chunk's embedding should know where it came from.

items.title: Citations and grounding
items.body:
## The answer must point at its sources
RAG's whole promise is answers grounded in real documents, not the model's memory, and the feature that delivers and proves that grounding is citations: every claim in the answer points to the specific retrieved chunk it came from. This matters for two reasons. Trust: a user (or you) can click through and verify the claim against the source, instead of taking the model's word. And debuggability: when an answer is wrong, citations tell you instantly whether retrieval failed (the right chunk was not there) or generation failed (the chunk was there and the model misused it). An uncited RAG answer is unverifiable and undebuggable; a cited one is both.

## How to get the model to cite
The mechanism combines prompt structure and output structure. You give the model the retrieved chunks with identifiers (number them, or tag each with its source), and instruct it to cite the chunk id after each claim it makes from the context.
```text
[1] (Vaswani et al., Methods) Self-attention computes ...
[2] (Vaswani et al., Results) On WMT-14 the model achieves ...

Question: How is attention computed and what did it achieve?
Answer with a [n] citation after each claim drawn from the sources.
```
The model then produces "Attention is computed by ... [1], achieving a BLEU of ... [2]." For reliability you often make this structured output (W6): a schema where each answer sentence carries its supporting chunk ids, so citations are guaranteed present and machine-checkable rather than something the model might forget. Some providers also offer built-in citation features that return source spans directly. Either way, the design is: number the sources, require a citation per claim, and prefer a structured format that enforces it.

## Grounding is also a discipline against hallucination
Citations are half of grounding; the other half is instructing the model to only answer from the provided context and to abstain when the answer is not there. A grounded RAG system, asked something its retrieved chunks do not cover, should say "the provided sources do not contain this" rather than confidently filling the gap from training data, which is exactly the dangerous failure RAG is supposed to prevent. So the system prompt does double duty: "answer using only the sources below, cite each claim, and if the sources do not contain the answer, say so." That instruction, plus the citation requirement, is what makes a RAG answer trustworthy, the model is constrained to the retrieved evidence and forced to show its work, and the ability to abstain is itself something you will test in next week's eval (questions with no answer in the corpus).

## Where this fits
Add numbered-source citations and a ground-only-in-the-sources-or-abstain instruction to your paper assistant, ideally as structured output so citations are guaranteed. You have made the assistant's answers verifiable and honest, which is the entire point of RAG over just asking the model, and you have built in the abstention behaviour that distinguishes a trustworthy answer system from a confident-sounding one.

items.title: Evaluation
items.body:
## You changed five things; did any of them help?
This week you added query rewriting, structure-aware chunking, reranking, contextual retrieval, and citations, each claiming to improve RAG. Here is the uncomfortable question: how do you know any of them actually helped? "The answers seem better" is not knowing, it is hoping, and it is exactly how teams ship a "smarter" pipeline that is quietly worse. This day is the bridge to next week: before you trust any RAG pattern, you need a way to measure whether a change improved or degraded quality, because a pipeline with five clever patterns and no measurement is five guesses stacked on top of each other.

## The two things RAG eval measures
RAG can fail at two distinct stages, and you measure them separately because the fix differs. Retrieval quality: did the system find the right chunks at all? If the relevant passage never made it into the context, no model can answer correctly, and that is a retrieval problem (fix chunking, the reranker, the query rewrite). Answer quality: given the retrieved chunks, did the model produce a correct, grounded answer? If the right chunk was retrieved but the answer is wrong or hallucinated, that is a generation problem (fix the prompt, the grounding instruction). Conflating them is why RAG debugging flails; separating "did we retrieve the right thing" from "did we answer well given what we retrieved" tells you where to fix, and it is the structure of the metrics you will build next week.

## Why you need a fixed test set, not vibes
The tool that turns "seems better" into "is better" is a golden test set: a fixed collection of questions with known correct answers and known source documents, that you run every pipeline variant against. With it, "I added reranking" becomes "reranking moved retrieval recall from 0.71 to 0.86 and answer correctness from 0.64 to 0.79", a real, comparable result. Without it, every change is evaluated on a different ad-hoc query and a gut feeling, so you cannot tell improvement from regression. Building that test set is real, manual work, and it is the most valuable thing you will build for RAG quality, which is exactly why next week is dedicated to doing it properly: the metrics, the test set, and the repeatable eval pipeline that lets you tune RAG with evidence instead of hope.

## Where this fits
Assemble a small handful of test questions with known answers for your paper assistant and use them to check whether your patterns helped, even informally. You have felt the core problem, you cannot improve a RAG pipeline you cannot measure, which is the entire motivation for next week. W12 turns this informal check into a proper evaluation discipline: real retrieval and answer metrics, a well-built golden set, and a CLI that scores any pipeline variant repeatably.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
A paper assistant that answers questions about real ArXiv papers, beyond naive RAG. By tonight:
- structure-aware chunking that respects the papers' sections, with sensible size and overlap.
- a retrieve-broadly-then-rerank pipeline (top-50 down to top-5) feeding the model.
- contextual retrieval so chunks carry their document context into the embedding.
- grounded, cited answers, every claim points to its source chunk, and the assistant abstains when the papers do not contain the answer.

## The test that proves it
The proof is a hard, real question answered correctly with verifiable citations, and an honest abstention. Ask your assistant a multi-part question about a paper ("what method does this propose and what's its main limitation?") that requires combining chunks from different sections, and check that the answer is correct, cites the specific passages, and that clicking the citations confirms each claim. Then ask something the paper does not address and confirm it abstains rather than inventing an answer. "It answered the two-part methods-and-limitations question with correct citations to the right sections, and refused to answer the out-of-scope question" is the deliverable, a RAG system that is accurate, verifiable, and honest about what it does not know.

## Ship the artifact
Commit the paper assistant with its chunking, retrieval-and-rerank pipeline, contextual retrieval, and citation/grounding, plus a README explaining each pattern and why it is there. This is a strong portfolio piece because it shows you go beyond the naive RAG that most people stop at, you can name a specific failure of naive retrieval and the specific pattern that fixes it. The citations especially signal maturity: they show you build RAG that is verifiable and honest, not a confident black box, which is exactly what distinguishes a production RAG engineer.

## Where this fits in the track
You can now build production-grade RAG: good chunks, two-stage retrieval, context-aware embeddings, and grounded, cited, abstaining answers, the patterns that make RAG actually work on real documents. But every pattern you added was justified by "it should help," and you have no rigorous proof. That is the unmissable gap this phase has been building toward: next week (RAG Evaluation) you learn to measure RAG properly, retrieval and answer metrics, a golden test set, a repeatable eval CLI, so you can tune the pipeline with evidence. An AI system you cannot evaluate is one you cannot trust or improve, and measurement is the discipline the whole production phase rests on.

weeks.title: RAG Evaluation, Measuring What Matters
weeks.context:
You have built RAG systems. Now you need to know whether they work. The answer is not "I tried it and the answers seemed reasonable." The answer is numbers: retrieval precision, context recall, answer faithfulness, answer relevance. This week you build a RAG eval CLI that runs a complete evaluation pipeline from a config file and outputs a structured report.

A golden test set is the foundation. Without ground truth, specific questions with known correct answers and known source documents, you cannot measure recall or faithfulness. Building the test set is manual work and it is the most important investment you make in eval quality. Spend time on it. Include questions where the answer is easy to find, questions where the answer requires combining two chunks, and questions that have no answer in the corpus (to test your system's ability to abstain).

Retrieval metrics measure whether your system is finding the right documents. Recall@k measures what fraction of relevant documents appear in the top-k results. Precision@k measures what fraction of the top-k results are actually relevant. NDCG (Normalised Discounted Cumulative Gain) accounts for position, a relevant document at rank 1 contributes more than one at rank 5. MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank) measures where the first relevant document appears.

Answer metrics measure whether the final answer is correct. Faithfulness measures whether the answer's claims are supported by the retrieved context, it catches hallucinations. Answer relevance measures whether the answer addresses the question asked. Correctness requires ground truth: does the answer contain the information in the expected answer?

The CLI architecture makes evaluation repeatable and configurable. Different config files test different pipeline variants: different chunking strategies, different top-k values, different models. Running the CLI on every code change tells you whether a change improved or degraded quality.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
You have built RAG systems and tuned them by feel. This week you replace feel with numbers. You build a RAG evaluation CLI: point it at a config file (which pipeline, which chunking, which model, which top-k) and a golden test set, and it runs the whole pipeline over every test question and outputs a structured report, retrieval precision and recall, answer faithfulness and relevance and correctness. By Sunday you can answer "is this RAG change an improvement or a regression?" with evidence, run it on every code change, and tune your pipeline the way you would tune any system you can measure. This is the week RAG stops being art and becomes engineering.

## Why "the answers seem reasonable" is a trap
The default way people evaluate RAG, ask it a few questions, eyeball the answers, conclude it works, fails for reasons that compound. You test on a handful of questions you happen to think of, which are not representative; you judge "reasonable" subjectively and inconsistently; and crucially, you have no baseline to compare a change against, so you cannot tell whether your new reranker helped, hurt, or did nothing. Worse, an answer that sounds fluent and confident can be completely wrong (a hallucination reads exactly like a correct answer), so "seems reasonable" actively misleads you. Measurement replaces all of that with a fixed test set, defined metrics, and comparable numbers, the only way to know if RAG works that survives contact with reality.

## The two halves: retrieval metrics and answer metrics
RAG eval mirrors the two failure stages from last week, and you measure each. Retrieval metrics ask "did we find the right documents?", recall (did the relevant chunks make it into the top-k?), precision (are the top-k actually relevant?), and rank-aware versions (does the best chunk come first?). Answer metrics ask "given what we retrieved, is the final answer good?", faithfulness (are the answer's claims supported by the context, i.e. is it hallucinating?), answer relevance (does it address the question?), and correctness (does it match the known right answer?). Splitting eval this way is what makes it actionable: a bad retrieval score and a bad answer score point you at completely different fixes, so the report does not just grade your RAG, it tells you which stage to work on.

## Where this fits
You build the eval CLI this week, the measurement discipline that the entire production phase rests on. It closes the RAG phase: you can now build production RAG (W11) and prove whether it works (W12). And the skill generalises immediately, evals are how you ship any AI feature with confidence (W17 makes them a deployment gate), because the lesson is universal: an AI system you cannot measure is one you cannot trust, improve, or responsibly put in front of users. RAG was the concrete case; eval is the discipline.

days.title: Building a golden test set
